#7728. 31 Vintage Christmas Ideas Worth Bringing Back This Year

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 2:14 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Festive feather trees, classic cocktails, and decorative popcorn garlands: Yesteryear’s Christmas revelers really knew how to embrace the holiday season. This year, add a festive touch of seasonal cheer to your home with these old-school traditions. These vintage Christmas decorations and comforting treats will impress any guest, and create lasting memories for years to come.

Christmas teas aren’t just for the British. This traditional activity, which came to America in the 1830s as part of the temperance movement, brought families together to converse while drinking a variety of teas at long communal tables. So, fire up the tea kettle, make some fancy finger sandwiches, and enjoy a warm mug of tea with your loved ones.

The first artificial Christmas tree, which was a feather tree, dates back to mid-19th-century Germany. The thin-branched trees became popular in America in the 1920s, when European immigrants carried their holiday traditions to their new homes. Add a feather tree to your holiday decor for a touch of whimsy and historical charm.

Best Choice’s 9-foot tree has over 2,000 branch tips, strong branches, and beautiful flocking. Read the review.

Classic cocktails have made a comeback in bars around the country. Learn how to make a few favorites so you’ll have something to keep yourself warm, and impress your guests, over the holidays. Good choices for winter include the hot toddy (made with a bracing spirit like brandy, rum, or whiskey mixed with honey, spices, and boiling water) and the Tom and Jerry (a concoction of eggnog, brandy, and rum). Pouring your potables into fancy cocktail glasses makes them even more festive.

Jell-O long ago lost its spot as the star of the dessert table, but we think it’s about time the jiggly treat made a comeback. Pull out one of your grandma’s old recipe books and have fun constructing your very own holiday Jell-O mold, sure to be a crowd-pleaser at the kids’ table this year.

When families in the 1950s and ’60s didn’t want to maintain real Christmas trees, they opted for aluminum versions instead. Nowadays, these shimmering trees can add a little sparkly elegance to your seasonal decor while giving a nod to a long-lost trend. National Tree Company’s red tinsel tree is fire resistant, 6 feet high and has a 20-inch base diameter.

Before people adorned their trees with lights and ornaments, they decorated them with homemade popcorn garlands. Strings of popped kernels were budget-friendly and simple to construct. This year, spend quality time with your kids, parents, or grandparents making your own vintage popcorn garland. Be sure to pop extra corn to munch on as you work!

In the past, people traditionally thanked their regular letter carriers by giving them a small Christmas gift. Though we don’t always have the chance to develop relationships with our letter carriers today, it’s still a nice idea to give them a token of appreciation around the holidays. Just remember that federal guidelines stipulate that postal employees can’t accept gifts worth more than $20.

Stockings overflow with chocolates and toys on Christmas morning, but in simpler times children were excited and grateful to find oranges in their stockings. Put an orange in your child’s stocking this year as a reminder of your family’s good fortune, and for a healthy dose of vitamin C.

Tinsel became popular in the United States in the 1950s as people sought a way to add shimmer to their Christmas trees without using Christmas lights, which were considered a fire hazard. Re-create this vintage trend and give your tree a shiny, icy look by draping strands of tinsel on the branches. (Skip this tradition if you have pets, because tinsel is a choking hazard for them.)

With roots in solstice celebrations of ancient times, caroling is one of the oldest holiday traditions in the world. Channel your jolly ancestors and spread holiday cheer by taking your family Christmas caroling this year. Don’t worry if your singing voice doesn’t rival Beyoncé’s—this tradition is more about having fun than showing off your vocal chops.

In the early 20th century, people relied on trains as a primary mode of transportation. It’s no wonder that toy versions of these all-important vehicles started appearing underneath Christmas trees during that time. Set up a track around your Christmas tree to take your holiday visitors back in time, or gift a toy train to young relatives.

With the convenience of Netflix and DVDs, it’s easy to forget that children used to have to wait all year for their favorite classic Christmas specials to air on TV, and how excited they’d get when that day finally rolled around. Re-create the joys of a less plugged-in era by looking up the air times of old favorites, such as “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” or “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” then whipping up a fresh batch of hot chocolate for a cozy night with the family.

Find a spot on the mantel for the classic figurines your family collected growing up, like Pixie Elves, Byers’ Choice Christmas Carolers, or Snowbabies. While the Elf on the Shelf might be the more common character right now, these guys were the original ones keeping watch over the house before Santa arrived.

If you don’t already have a Christmas village collection, consider starting one this year. The tradition of collecting miniature structures can be traced all the way back to the 17th century, but the charming ceramic houses and stores you know and love kicked off in the 1970s. Today, it’s easy to search up online sites and forums where Christmas village enthusiasts share their tips and tricks for creating elaborate setups.

We sing about it every year, but have you ever actually had a roasted chestnut? On a weekend afternoon or cozy evening, try your hand at roasting chestnuts—a stovetop will work just as well as an open fire for this.

Everything old is new again, and that includes ceramic Christmas trees. This ’70s Christmas decoration has roared back into style. If you don’t have one collecting dust in the basement, you can find the 15-inch Best Choice Products pre-lit ceramic Christmas tree, 18-inch Mr. Christmas ceramic tree, and others like them online.

If you have ever been to or seen photos of Dyker Heights Christmas lights, then you’re familiar with blow mold Christmas decorations. The playful plastic figurines first popped up on the market in the 1930s. Although many folks today like Christmas inflatables, we believe there’s enough room on the lawn for both.

Over the top, but worth it: BZB Goods’ Santa Claus with sleigh is 12 feet long and illuminated with internal lights.

While there are plenty of modern holiday hits to enjoy, set a retro mood by putting together a playlist with tracks from the likes of Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra. While music-streaming services like Spotify already have plenty of holiday playlists to choose from, you can also curate a selection that reminds you of Christmases past.

Snail mail is so retro! Virtual Christmas greetings get the job done, but they aren’t nearly as sentimental as old-fashioned handwritten cards. Crisp stationery and seasonal stamps never fail to spread holiday cheer. Buy a boxed card set, or take a picture with your kids (or pet!) and incorporate it into a personalized greeting for everyone on your mailing list.

While it’s convenient to pick up a freshly cut Christmas tree from a big-box store’s parking lot, the tradition doesn’t have quite the same sense of holiday magic as venturing into a snow-covered wood to choose the perfect type of Christmas tree for your home. Depending on where you live, there are likely Christmas tree farms in your area that allow you to choose and cut down your own Christmas tree.

In the Middle Ages, the Lord of Misrule was a figure who was appointed to take charge of planning the Christmas activities in royal courts and noble houses. But this tradition came with a twist: The “Lord” often planned holiday pranks and jests. Try out this historic practice in your home this holiday season by giving children turns being the Lord of Misrule for the day. Allow the “Lord” to decide which treats to eat after dinner, which holiday special to watch, or letting them arrange the Elf on the Shelf for the following day.

While today’s Christmas supper typically features turkey or ham as a main dish, goose was once the centerpiece of many holiday dinner tables. In fact, eating goose for Christmas is a tradition that dates back to ancient Greece. A goose may be tricky to track down, but it’s generally possible to order one in advance from a high-quality butcher.

Tiny warm white lights are most common nowadays—on the tree and outside—but why not decorate with some retro flair? The big, colorful light bulbs you remember from previous decades are now available ineco-friendly LED bulbs. The burst of color outlining your house will make your home stand out from everyone else’s on the block.

With 3-inch C9 LED bulbs, the indoor/outdoor C9 LED lights from Wintergreen 17-foot strings really dazzle when used to frame the roof,

Today, getting dressed up for Christmas dinner typically means showing up in pair of elastic-waist pants to accommodate second helpings of turkey. In photos of midcentury Christmases, however, you’ll likely see men in ties and women in chic dresses with nary a pair of sweatpants in sight. Update your holiday dress code this year to bring back some vintage holiday glamour.

Evoke a vintage Christmas vibe by watching some holiday classics this December. Introduce your family to some timeless black-and-white picks like Miracle on 34th Street, White Christmas, and It’s a Wonderful Life. If you’re already familiar with these classics, screen an underrated holiday flick like Christmas in Connecticut or I’ll Be Seeing You.

Christmas crackers first made an appearance in Victorian England and are still popular in the U.K., but aren’t common on American holiday tables. A cracker is a wrapped cardboard tube that makes a loud cracking sound when pulled at both ends. They typically contain paper crowns as well as a small trinket and a card containing a joke or a piece of trivia, all of which are great dinnertime icebreakers.

You’re probably familiar with the “12 Days of Christmas” tradition because of the popular yuletide carol, but it’s a tradition that has largely died out in North America. Christians traditionally celebrated from December 25 to January 5 or 6, and gave one another small gifts each day. Extend the holiday season in your home by keeping festivities alive until Twelfth Night and continue to enjoy Christmas treats and festive holiday movies.

Though in many ways Christmas has become commercialized, you can bring back the spirit of giving that the holiday season once held by lending a hand to your neighbors or community. Help an elderly neighbor hang Christmas lights, volunteer at a toy drive for underprivileged children, or spend a day working at a soup kitchen to spread holiday cheer to those who need it most.

The origin of bottle brush Christmas trees dates back to the 1940s when, as the story goes, Addis Housewares Company manufactured the trees on the same machines the company used to make toilet brushes. Addis never did confirm the truth of the tree’s manufacture, but we’ll never look at a toilet brush the same way again. Though vintage version of these faux-snow-covered trees are hard to come by, you can find reproductions at retailers like Target and Crate and Barrel.

#7727. 8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”

Plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”

Failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, says HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the issue, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

“Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

#7724. The Butler Didn't Do It

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Todd Butler's bare Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire.

Todd Butler has now posted his questionnaire for the Senate Judiciary Committee. Here is the chronology Butler offers for his nomination:

On June 29, 2026, Senator Roger Wicker contacted me about a potential vacancy on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. I spoke with Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith the following day. On July 1, 2026, an official from the White House Counsel's Office contacted me to arrange an interview. On July 13, 2026, I interviewed with officials from the White House Counsel's Office. Following my interview, I received periodic updates from Senator Wicker about the process. On October I, 2026, President Trump called to inform me that he planned to nominate me for a position on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

There is a very relevant date missing here. On September 28, 2026, Judge Southwick publicly announced that he would take senior status. Yet three months earlier, Senator Wicker contacted Butler about the potential vacancy.

As I said from the outset, the fix was in. There was some sort of deal involving Wicker, Southwick, and the White House. I'm sure this interview was pro forma. and doubt any other candidates were interviewed. Judge Southwick could have announced his intentions at any time in August or early September, but he waited until the last possible moment to jam up the process, and ensure Butler would not go down. I do hope at least one Senator asks Butler if he is aware of any communications in which Judge Southwick, directly or indirectly, conditioned his willingness to take senior status if Butler is the nominee.

As for the rest of the SJQ, let's just say Butler's pantry is bare. Or, the Butler didn't do it.

Butler went to law school between 2005 and 2008, but he wasn't a member of the Federalist Society. That makes sense, as he wrote critically of Justice Scalia, originalism, and the Second Amendment. He wasn't a member while he clerked. Indeed, he didn't become a member of the Federalist Society until 2016. I suspect lots of people joined before or after Trump's victory. It would help with career prospects. He has never held any leadership positions in FedSoc. But rest assured that he was active in the Inn of Court and the Mississippi Bar, holding several leadership positions.

Butler has extensive experience in employment law. In addition to the publications I flagged, Butler speaks and writes often about the EEOC, FLSA, and related topics of municipal law. His only professional exposure to constitutional law involves defendant local officials who are sued for violating First Amendment rights. After Olivier v. City of Brandon, his most significant case was as defense counsel in a wrongful death case. He taught at the Mississippi College of Law "periodic[ally]" between 2008 and 2016 but does not recall which semesters he taught. He also does not have copies of the syllabi.

Here is how Butler describes his pro bono work:

Over the course of my career, I have accepted pro bono clients, typically through the Mission First Legal Aid Clinic or the Mississippi Volunteers Lawyers Project. I have assisted with adoptions, child visitation matters, and other domestic issues. I also have provided pro bono services to a local church, including contract review and procedure drafting, in connection with the operation of a faith-based children's center. I advised a local pastor on a land acquisition that he is considering using for a fellowship facility. And I have volunteered, along with others at my law firm, at Stewpot Community Services, where we served meals to people experiencing homelessness.

There is no pro bono work that would remotely be associated with the conservative legal movement. And no, working for a church does not necessarily make a person conservative.

If I were to show you this questionnaire, without any knowledge of Mississippi politics, would you possibly think this was a viable record for the Fifth Circuit? No.

#7723. 13 Potted Plants You Can—and Should—Winter Indoors

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:31 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plenty of gardeners place their houseplants outdoors for the summer and enjoy them indoors the rest of the year. So why not try a similar strategy, and save a little money while you’re at it, by bringing your favorite cold-tender plants inside when the temperature drops so they’ll be ready to grow again when spring and summer rolls around?

Before you bring your outdoor plants in for the winter, you’ll need to do a bit of preparation. Start by inspecting them for pests and treating, if necessary. Repot if a plant needs it, and cut down on (or eliminate) fertilizing. Some plants can simply be brought indoors as houseplants, others should be forced into dormancy for a few months of cool storage, and still others are best kept going by making rooted cuttings. The following are a few cold-tender plants that you can bring inside each winter and then continue to enjoy outside for many summers to come.

While some palm trees are hardy in the winters of the Deep South, most palms need help to survive winter temperatures, even only to 55 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit . It’s possible to cover and winterize some palms planted in the ground, but potted palms should come indoors (preferably to a bright, humid spot). Move palms to an indoor location that gets lots of light. Water them regularly to keep the soil moist until spring, and carry them back outdoors after nights warm back up to at least 50 or 60 degrees.

Leave cacti outdoors as late into the season as possible so that the combination of shorter days and cooler nights will stimulate a dormancy response. You’ll need to keep an eye on the thermometer and know the low-temperature threshold for your particular type of cactus. Some species may be able to withstand 20-degree temperatures, but others cannot. If unsure, move potted cacti indoors as soon as cold drops to about 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

Stop watering cacti 3 to 4 weeks before the move so the plants are dry, and check them carefully for pets like mealy bugs or mites. In general, cacti do best in a cool location with minimal water, as they go dormant. Transition them back outside in early spring, gradually introducing sunlight if the plants show any sign of burning.

Citrus trees can actively grow and flower in winter, and may also ripen fruit if they’re pollinated. Even without winter growth, it’s a good idea protect these plants during the chilly months. As the days get shorter, move potted citrus trees (typically, dwarf varieties of lime and lemon trees) to an interim space outdoors that gets some protection from the elements, like a porch with radiant heat, and cut back on watering.

Before the first frost, move the citrus tree into a brightly lit indoor room, ideally between 55 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Citrus plants are sensitive to the drying effects of air, so it’s best to position them away from heat vents and cold drafts. Provide supplemental humidity with a pebble tray or regular misting.

Move tropical hibiscus plants indoors when overnight temperatures reach the low 50s. Place them in a brightly lit room, and treat them like regular houseplants. Cut back on watering and fertilizing during these cooler months. Try to avoid heat vents and cold drafts, and put the plants on a pebble tray to boost the ambient humidity, if necessary. Prune tropical hibiscus three times during late fall and winter (October, December, and February) to maintain the plant’s shape.

Prune jasmine vines by at least 25 percent before bringing them in for winter, letting them adjust gradually by bringing them inside at night and slowly lengthening the time spent indoors. Some or all of the plant’s leaves will fall off, but new ones will grow again in time. Bring jasmine into a sunny room before frosty weather arrives, and keep it away from drying air vents and drafts. Use a pebble tray to boost humidity to about 30 percent.

Coleus plants are grown for their stunning foliage and adaptability to shade. The plants are annuals in most regions, though, since they do not like temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit and cannot survive temperatures below freezing. Bring the potted plant indoors once nights hover near 50 degrees. Repot the plant if it is outgrowing its container.

Another option is to propagate coleus stems to use next spring. Cut a 6-inch healthy stem, remove low leaves, and dip the stem in a rooting hormone before planting it in a container with moist potting mix. Cover the container with a plastic bag for a few weeks and keep it in a warm and sunny spot; water regularly.

Aromatic rosemary is a favorite cooking herb for many fall and winter dishes. However, the plant does not always survive winters in USDA Zones 6 or lower. Start by planting a rosemary in a well-draining container. Bring potted rosemary indoors before the first freeze. Keep it in a cool location with fairly high humidity, but avoid overwatering; if its roots stay damp and cool, it can develop root rot.

Feel free to harvest from the plant, but never cut off more than about 20 percent of the foliage and avoid cutting into woody main stems. You also can propagate rosemary indoors at the end of the season with 4- to 6-inch cuttings from a stem with no flowers.

Elephant ears, or taro, is a tropical plant that can survive a light frost only; a true freeze will kill the tuber. Simply move potted elephant ears indoors to a cool bright location. For those grown in the ground, carefully dig up the elephant ear tuber when cool weather approaches and the foliage dies back (they won’t survive winter outdoors in USDA Zone 6 and lower). Cut stems down to about 4 to 6 inches, and gently wipe off excess dirt.

Place the tuber in a warm, dark location with good air circulation to dry out for a few days. Wrap the bulbs in paper or drop them in a paper bag and store them in a cool, dry, dark place. Check them periodically for rot (throw rotten ones away) and insect damage (treat with an insecticide). Beware that nearly all its parts are toxic to pets and people if ingested—we don’t recommend bringing it indoors if you have young children.

It is technically possible to bring Boston ferns indoors and overwinter them in their active state, but it gets very messy very quickly. Instead, let them rest. Put them in a cool, moderately light to dark location that will not freeze, like an unheated basement or garage.

Before bringing your fern inside, hose it down on a warm (60-degree Fahrenheit) day to spray away insects and loose leaves. Give it a light trim, and shake and ruffle the fronds to drop debris before carrying the plant to its indoor spot. Moisten dry soil as needed until spring. Don’t be alarmed if some leaves pale or drop.

Geranium is another plant that likes to sleep the winter away. Dig the plants out of the ground before the first freeze, and gently knock the soil off the roots. Allow the plants to dry in a cool, shady location for a couple of days. Place the plants upside down in a paper bag and close the top. Store them in a cool, dark location that stays between 55 and 60 degrees.

About 2 months before the last frost date, trim the stored geraniums and plant them in moist potting soil with two leaf nodes below the soil line. You also can propagate cuttings or bring potted geraniums indoors to a sunny window.

Thyme is a flavorful and aromatic perennial herb, but a tender one in regions 5 or lower. Plant culinary thyme in a container in spring, keeping it in a sunny, bright location with well-draining soil. Bring it indoors for winter before the first frost. If the herb’s roots are peeking though the bottom of the pot or it looks crowded, repot the thyme when you bring it in. It also can be divided easily.

Be sure to place the container near a sunny window with a western or southern exposure in a room that maintains a 60- to 70-degrees Fahrenheit temperature for most of the day. Prune or pinch off flowers to preserve the herb’s flavor. Water as needed, allowing the container dry out between watering. You can fertilize every week or two with a diluted solution of fish emulsion or liquid seaweed. Harvest sprigs as needed for winter dishes.

Although Musa basjoo, Musella lasiocarpa, and a few other banana trees are quite cold hardy, most will not tolerate extended freezing temperatures. Potted banana plants can be brought indoors to a bright, sunny room to spend the winter in a slowed active state. They can take up some space indoors, so you also can help them sleep through winter. As the weather cools, gradually reduce watering. Before the first frost, cut the plant to 6 inches in height and move it to a dark, cool location. Keep the soil just moist until the weather warms in the spring.

The stunning evergreen cordyline is hardy only in the warmest growing zones, but potted cordylines can be moved indoors when temperatures dip into the 60s. Place them in a spot with good ventilation and consistent indoor temperatures; avoid placing them near air vents or in drafty areas. Increase humidity around cordyline by situating it in a humid room or on a saucer filled with pebbles and water, and avoid fluoride-treated tap water. Although the plant does not require dormancy in winter, it does like a rest, so cut water some during fall and winter.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7722. What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

The holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

“TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”

Manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

The holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

Want to retain a high level of insulation power but don’t want to work with fiberglass and all the safety precautions that go along with it? Check out this water heater blanket from SmartJacket. In choosing the best water heater blankets among those currently on the market, we looked at two top factors: material and size. Our list of recommendations covers the most popular types of water heater blanks, including thick fiberglass options as well as thinner foam and foil options.

We also made sure to include a range of sizes on our list with options to cover most water heater shapes. For oddly shaped water heaters with awkward piping, we included recommendations for several easy-to-cut options that can fit snugly around even the most difficult water heater shapes or those in tight spaces.

Before shopping for a water heater blanket, read this section to understand the factors and features to keep in mind. This will help you make an informed decision.

When perusing water heater blankets, you’ll notice that there are a few different types available. This mostly comes down to the type of insulating material. Some are easier to work with during installation than others, as they often need to be trimmed to fit individual water heaters.

You may also find combinations of materials, such as fiberglass insulation with a foil face. This can offer the best of both worlds, as it uses a thick, insulating layer of air pockets and radiates heat back into the tank.

Water heaters, like most appliances, come in different sizes. The size of house and family and the number of sinks and showers all affect how large a water heater a home needs. While water heaters range between 30 and 98 gallons, 40-, 50-, and 60-gallon tanks are the common sizes used in homes.

Water heater blankets also come in similar sizes, so it’s important to find one that will work for your tank. If you have a 50-gallon tank, finding a water heater blanket to fit it should be no problem. Water heater blankets large enough to fit 98-gallon tanks, commonly found in commercial settings, may be harder to track down.

When it comes to materials such as fiberglass, cotton, and denim, the thicker the water heater blanket, the better it will be at insulating. A water heater located in a cool basement calls for a thicker blanket. Thicker blankets will do a better job of separating the cool air and the heat radiating from the tank than thinner ones.

Because foil works primarily by reflecting the heat instead of relying on an air-pocket barrier, it needn’t be thick to function efficiently. Most water heater blankets made with foil are less than ½ inch thick, which is another reason foil water heater blankets are so easy to work with.

Just like your home’s insulation, water heater blankets come in a variety of insulation ratings. These ratings are described as R-value, where the R stands for resistance. The higher the R-value, the more resistance the insulation has against heat transfer. Essentially, more is better.

The highest R-value you’re likely to find for a residential water heater blanket is R-11, but values of R-7 and R-8 are more common. To get the most from your investment, it’s best to use the water heater blanket with the highest R-value.

It’s important to keep in mind, though, that foil-type insulation rarely offers an R-value; R-values apply to fiberglass and other similar types of insulation.

Water heaters have burner assemblies that get very hot. The point of insulating a water heater is to save energy and money, not cause a fire. Different water heater blanket materials have varying degrees of fire resistance to combat that risk. While the most common designation is Class 1/Class A, it’s helpful to know which types are the most fire resistant.

If fire resistance is of utmost importance, a fiberglass or foil water heater blanket is the way to go. Some fiberglass or foil products aren’t fire rated, but that doesn’t mean they’re unsafe. Just be sure to keep the insulation clear of the burner by a few inches.

There are two types of water heaters: electric and gas. Electric water heaters have a heating element inside that energizes and heats the water that surrounds it. Gas water heaters have burners underneath that kick on to heat water through convection.

Fortunately, water heater blankets are interchangeable between the two water heater types. However, if you have a gas-powered heater, it’s crucial that the blanket doesn’t cover or otherwise obstruct the flue (aka exhaust) at the top. If you have an electric model, the blanket must not cover or obstruct its control box or access panel, typically located on the side of the tank. Also, be sure to cut the insulation back from the burner by at least 2 inches while installing.

For additional information about buying and using the best water heater blanket, consider the answers to these frequently asked questions.

A great water heater blanket will offer a blend of insulation value, cost-effectiveness, and fire resistance.

It depends on the size of your tank. Generally speaking, manufacturers label their water heater blankets according to the size of the tank they’ll cover. If you’re unsure, measure your tank’s height and circumference, and compare it to the measurements on the package.

Water heater blankets are low maintenance, but fiberglass, cotton, and denim can begin to smell and stop insulating if they get wet. It’s a good idea to check on your water heater blanket a few times a year to ensure it’s still in good condition.

Undamaged water heater blankets may far outlast a water heater. The average gas water heater lasts between 8 and 12 years, while the average electric water heater lasts 10 to 15 years. A water heater blanket kept in good condition will outlast a water heater without issue.

The most efficient way to install a water heater blanket is to measure the height and circumference of your tank before unrolling the product, allowing for an extra 2 inches for the circumference so you can overlap the product. Premeasuring allows you to swiftly cut the product to size using cutter or scissors. Wrap the tank with the blanket, and secure it in place with foil tape placed vertically along the seam. Cover the top of the tank with two half circles of material, and secure it in place with foil tape. Ensure that you cut openings for the venting hood, pressure relief valve, burner access cover, and wiring connection box. Make the holes about 2 inches larger than each opening to allow airflow.

Yes. Any steps you can take to keep your water hot without additional reheating of the water is worth it. The water heater blanket does just this and is an inexpensive purchase. In most cases, you should be able to recoup your investment when installing an insulator blanket.

Yes. When properly installed, hot water heater blankets are safe to use. The most important thing is to ensure proper airflow around all fixtures by cutting slightly larger openings around valves, hoods, burners, etc. Don’t forget that some blankets contain fiberglass, and those installing the product should wear safety goggles, a dust mask, gloves, and long sleeves, then carefully clean the area after installation to remove any stray fiberglass fibers.

#7720. Elon Musk Is Pulling the Plug on Cybertrucks to Focus on Something New

Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The company’s CEO Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the company is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

In a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality issues, as well as several safety recalls.

Current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

For anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

#7718. S. Ct. Suspends District Court's Injunction Blocking Border Barrier Building

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"There is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim."

From today's Supreme Court unsigned opinion in Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church (with Justice Jackson essentially dissenting):

Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secretary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct border barriers and roads "to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States." The same section expressly authorizes the Secretary "'to waive all legal requirements'" as "'necessary to ensure expeditious construction'" of those barriers and roads, and sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations. Specifically, the statute provides that "'[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States'" and courts "'shall not have jurisdiction'" over nonconstitutional claims. §102(c)(2)(A).

Earlier this year, the Secretary invoked Section 102's waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at the U.S.–Mexico border, in a region that U.S. Customs and Border Protection has designated the "Big Bend Sector." The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector "is an area of high illegal entry" requiring additional border barriers, and waived the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws to facilitate expeditious construction.

Shortly thereafter, respondents—an individual river guide, an environmental nonprofit, and a nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas—challenged those waiver determinations by filing suit in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas. Respondents claimed, among other things, that the Secretary's waiver determinations "violat[ed] the major questions doctrine under the U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 1." Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers.

On October 2, 2026, the District Court entered a preliminary injunction blocking the Secretary's waivers and halting all associated construction. The District Court acknowledged that its jurisdiction was limited to constitutional claims. But it nonetheless concluded that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" qualified because, in its view, the "major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear statement rule grounded in separation of powers." The court further held that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" was likely to succeed on the merits because the Secretary lacked "'clear congressional authorization' to issue" the waivers. Because the Fifth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear this case, IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(C), the Solicitor General filed an application requesting either summary reversal or a stay of the District Court's preliminary injunction.

We grant the requested stay. The Government is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument that the District Court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate respondents' so-called major-questions-doctrine claim. However it is labeled, respondents' claim does not "'alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,'" the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate. IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(A). It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recognized that "claims simply alleging" that the Executive Branch has exceeded its "statutory authority are not 'constitutional' claims." Dalton v. Specter (1994).

That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plaintiff invokes the major-questions doctrine. Many canons and rules of statutory interpretation reflect constitutional principles, including "constitutional avoidance, the clear-statement federalism rules, and the presumption against retroactivity." When courts invoke those canons, however, they do so in service of adjudicating statutory claims, not constitutional ones. The same is true when a court invokes "the major questions canon of statutory interpretation." There is no such thing as a "constitutional" major-questions claim….

Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress's enactment of IIRIRA §102(c)—which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws—reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert. And courts "of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute." The Government's interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents….

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 10, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

If you’ve ever tried to start your car, but the battery was dead, or you found a tire was too low to drive on, you may have wished for a jump starter air compressor. These combo tools claim to be able to get you going again—so we decided to put 11 of the top models to the test on our own vehicles, and found 7 that we can recommend. DeWalt’s 1600A Jump Starter with Air Compressor took top honors in our tests, thanks to its quality build, internal alternator tester, and convenient pressure presets for accurate inflation.

These devices bring enough voltage and amperage to bring a dead battery back to life. They can also fill a low tire or pump up a leaky one until the driver can make it to a service station for repairs. Ahead, learn the most important factors to consider when choosing one of these combo units and find out how the following models earned a spot on our lineup of the best jump starters with air compressors.

Bottom line: Jump starters with air compressors are essential tools for emergencies, offering reliable performance and versatility. DeWalt leads the pack with its superior features.

There might be a lot to know about these versatile devices, but shopping for the best jump starter with an air compressor doesn’t have to be complicated. To help make the process even easier, these top-rated products are an excellent starting point. We performed hands-on testing with every model listed below to ensure they can meet the grade.

The DeWalt jump starter/compressor combo performed flawlessly in our hands-on tests, easily earning the title of the best overall model. This unit supplies enough juice to start depleted batteries and has a built-in alternator tester.

We got an alternator reading by connecting it to a vehicle’s battery terminals when the vehicle was idling. Since problems starting a vehicle can be due to a faulty alternator, this feature is a nice perk.

The clamps are large and grip the terminals firmly. We were able to get a reading of the current battery voltage. When we connected the terminals to a fully charged battery, the DeWalt indicated the voltage, which is a good way to see the battery’s current charge.

The compressor measured the existing pressure in the tires. We were able to preselect the amount of air we wanted to add, and the compressor inflated the tires to the exact pressure. This handy feature removes the guesswork, especially when inflating bicycle tires that can explode if too much pressure is applied. It took about 20 seconds to inflate bike tires and about 5 minutes to inflate a large pickup tire.

What our tester says: “The DeWalt jump starter was a dream to use—its multifunctionality and high-quality performance made jumping batteries and filling tires almost effortless.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the DeWalt jump starter with air compressor at Tractor Supply Co., Amazon, or The Home Depot.

Jump starters with air compressors can be incredibly versatile, and this model from DieHard definitely fits the bill. The lead-acid jump starter offers 950 peak amps for cranking over large diesel engines as well as reverse hookup protection to avoid damaging the expensive electrical components that are sometimes vulnerable during jumping. It also features two 12V ports and a USB port for charging devices.

The compressor produces up to 150 PSI of pressure and includes a digital gauge for presetting the pressure and checking the battery’s charge level. A built-in work light makes working on the side of the road in low light a bit less difficult as well. This DieHard model also includes three air nozzle adapters for filling sports equipment, pool floats, and other items.

The DieHard jump starter was more than capable of firing up an old Land Rover. It was easier to attach than other models as the cables were slightly longer than the compact versions. And just a flip of the switch turned the unit on for the jumping function. We found that the air compressor worked well, pumping up the tire faster than the other full-size models (about 5 minutes faster from 20 PSI to 36 PSI), though the gauge is in a strange place—it’s right behind the positive clamp. Also, the battery gauge on the front of the unit isn’t all that detailed, providing only broad ranges: 70 to 100 percent, 30 to 70 percent, and under 30 percent.

Get the DieHard jump starter with air compressor at Ace Hardware.

The Trekure jump starter fits a lot of energy into a small package, making it a good option for taking along on road trips. We didn’t have any problems jump-starting three different dead batteries, but the clamps are a little on the small side—we would have appreciated larger clamps.

This unit came with some battery charge, but once it was depleted by testing, it took about 6 hours to recharge. We liked its bright LED flashlight, which allowed us to see what we were doing after dark. The flashlight also doubles as a yellow flashing road flare that can be seen from a distance.

The inflator aired up our bicycle and car tires but didn’t have quite the oomph to fill up larger truck tires. But it’s simple to use—the display screen let us choose from images of a car, motorcycle, bike, or basketball for adjusting air pressure.

We like the Trekure for all-purpose 12-volt jump-starting, but we think it’s best suited for light-duty tire inflation. It comes in a handy case and includes two USB ports and a plug-in DC outlet for charging various devices in the car.

Get the Trekure jump starter with air compressor at Amazon.

Folks who value versatility will want to consider the Schumacher SJ1332 rechargeable power station. This device features 1,200A of cranking power, allowing it to start a massive 8-liter gas engine or a 6-liter diesel engine. The Schumacher features two 12-volt (V) charging ports, two standard 120V outlets, and a USB port for charging mobile devices. This allows it to charge several devices or act as an emergency power station if the power goes out in the home. Its cables wrap around the unit and clip onto the base for storage, and the compressor hose stores in a small compartment in the back.

We weren’t big fans of the tire pressure gauge, which was not lit and wasn’t very accurate (a difference of around 8 PSI), and it’s in a weird spot (on the back of the jump pack and obscured by the clamp). But otherwise, the unit had plenty of power to jump the car and it was easy to use. We liked the 120V outlets.

What our tester says: “The Schumacher was relatively easy to use to jump my Land Rover. The light was helpful and allowed me to identify the cables easily at night, and the buttons and controls were fairly intuitive.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

For an additional well-rounded jump starter, Stanley’s J5C09 portable power station could fit the bill. This jump starter features a lead-acid battery with up to 10,000A of cranking power for turning over large engines in gasoline and diesel vehicles alike. This unit provides some additional built-in features worth noting. It offers a USB port for charging devices, a standard 12V port, a reverse polarity alarm to indicate improperly installed clamps, and a positionable work light for shedding light on the repair area.

During the test, the one feature that stood out the most was the air compressor. It was able to fill a tire in much less time than the other models (about 4 minutes), and the analog display was very accurate. It’s also easy to set up and use in the dark, plus it features extra-long cables to make reaching battery terminals easier. It also had plenty of power to kick the vehicle’s engine over. Get the Stanley jump starter with air compressor at MSC or Staples.

If you’re looking for a multi-function jump starter/compressor combo, check out this new model from JackPak. Right out of the box, we were impressed with this unit’s build quality—it’s solid, rugged, and comes with heavy-duty clamps.

Like the DeWalt that earned our best overall award, the JackPak shows how many volts the current vehicle battery has, which is great if there isn’t a voltmeter handy. We wish all the units came with this feature.

It supplied enough juice to jump all three dead batteries and took less than three hours to recharge. The compressor feature inflated our bike, car, and truck tires, but it took nearly 30 minutes to completely fill the truck tire. We liked the bright LED light on the JackPak, and it doubles as a powerbank for charging devices. It also features a low-power sleep mode that keeps its internal battery from discharging for up to 36 months.

Get the JackPack jump starter with air compressor at Lowe’s or The Home Depot.

When a battery goes dead and a car is stuck in a parking lot or across town (or the side of the road), there’s a lot on the line. We know that, so we tested the jump starters with air compressors on our own depleted car and truck batteries and to inflate a range of tires.

We tested each product by jumping a dead car, truck, and riding mower batteries. We also used a multimeter to determine the voltage from the jump starters. We tested the jump starters over a 2-week period, connecting each one to the various battery terminals and then attempting to start the vehicle.

We also drained some of the air from bike, car, and truck tires to test the built-in compressors. For the inflation tests, we partially deflated bike, car, and truck tires and then timed how long it took each inflator to return the tires to the recommended pressure. During these inflation tests, we paid close attention to how easily the air chucks connected to the valve stems, whether they created a secure seal, and how well they held up through repeated use. We also considered whether the compressors operated consistently under pressure or showed signs of strain, as well as how intuitive and responsive the controls were throughout the process.

We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a jump starter/inflator did on a test or assessment, the higher the points. The products that excelled were given awards based on their strengths, while those that failed were removed from our lineup.

Carrying a jump starter with an air compressor means drivers can handle emergencies and repairs without calling for help (or when help isn’t available). And who doesn’t enjoy a little self-reliance? These devices include built-in jumper cables to clamp onto the positive and negative terminals of a dead battery. It sounds straightforward, but shopping for one of these devices requires a bit of background and know-how. The following sections will break down the most important considerations to keep in mind while shopping for a battery jumper with air compressor.

Jump starters equipped with air compressors include one of two battery types: lithium-ion and lead-acid.

The best jump starters with air compressors—and all portable jump starters, for that matter—have an onboard battery that provides ample power to start a vehicle or operate the compressor. In most cases, the battery size of these portable chargers is described in milliampere hours (mAh) or amp hours (Ah)—1,000mAh equals 1Ah.

Higher mAh or Ah ratings equals a larger capacity to store power, so higher ratings mean more batteries charged and tires inflated between recharges. Generally speaking, most portable jump starters use batteries between 10,000 and 35,000mAh. Remember that higher capacity batteries are heavy, and get heavier as the storage increases.

The purpose of a jump starter is to provide a vehicle with enough power to turn over and fire up the engine, then allow the vehicle’s alternator to continue charging the battery. The amount of power a jump starter needs to accomplish this task is determined by the engine.

Small gasoline engines, such as four-cylinder engines found in most cars (and progressively larger vehicles) don’t require much power. But larger eight-cylinder engines require a bit more. And, because of the extremely high compression ratios of diesel engines, large models found in heavy-duty pickups, RVs, and power equipment require even more power. In general, 1,000A or more will do the trick.

Many manufacturers today don’t explicitly list the amount of power provided by their chargers. Instead, they discuss the types of engines their chargers can handle. This is only a concern for diesel vehicles, as any jump starter will handle most gasoline engines.

While it might seem that jumper cables are all created equal, modern jump starters offer additional safety features. Today’s models protect a vehicle’s electrical system and the person using the cables from sparking or reverse polarity, which happens when the user connects the clamps to the wrong terminals—something that’s very easy to do in the dark. Reverse polarity can wreak havoc on the sensitive electronics in today’s vehicles, so this is a crucial feature.

These units will detect the reverse polarity or contact between the clamps and prevent the unit from expelling stored energy through them. Often, a small light or audible alarm will alert the user so you can understand what’s occurring and why the jump starter isn’t charging the vehicle.

When choosing the best jump starter with an air compressor, there is some variance in the amount of pounds per square inch (PSI) offered by these models. Most models produce around 100 PSI—more than enough for any road vehicle’s tires. Most vehicle tires require just 30 to 40 PSI.

Some models offer 150 PSI or more, which is as much pressure as a traditional home air compressor. Are they necessary for typical vehicle repairs? No. But it might take these compressors less time to boost up a tire on the side of the road, so they could be worth the consideration and splurge.

Several additional features might make a portable jump starter with an air compressor a bit more attractive to consumers.

Even with all of this background on choosing the best jump starter with air compressor, you might have questions. The following section is a collection of some of the most frequently asked questions about battery jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.stions about jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.

#7715. Andrew McCarthy on the Hegseth Impeachment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A prominent conservative legal commentator explains why Hegseth should be convicted on at least some of the charges.

Yesterday, I wrote about why Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth deserves to be impeached and convicted for his role in in starting an unconstitutional war and perpetrating over 200 cases of outright murder with the "drug boat" strikes. Today GOP Rep. Thomas Massie filed impeachment charges in the House of Representatives. Even if they don't pass in the narrowly Republican-controlled lame duck Congress, they will almost certainly do so in the incoming Democratic one. Meanwhile prominent conservative legal commentator, national security law expert and former federal prosecutor Andrew McCarthy has published an excellent overview of the charges in the National Review.

McCarthy is far to my right, and far more sympathetic to the War on Drugs (I myself believe it should be abolished). Thus, it's notable that he and I agree that Hegseth should be convicted for his role in the drug boat strikes, which McCarthy characterizes as "indefensible":

I do not believe there is any viable justification for the extrajudicial killings by military force of operators of suspected drug boats. Drug trafficking is a crime, not an act of war. Our law addresses it through trial and imprisonment, not the use of military force…. The administration has not proved that the boats were ferrying narcotics, much less that the drugs were headed to the United States. The president's designation of Venezuelan criminal gangs as foreign terrorist organizations, besides being legally dubious (drug dealing is not "terrorist activity" as defined in federal law), does not authorize the use of force (it instead makes material support to the organization a crime and helps the government cut off funding sources). While the unauthorized killings in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific have not drawn the level of public ire that the Iran war has, they are indefensible, and Hegseth has been their loudest, crudest champion.

As noted in my earlier post, this view is similar to that of John Yoo, well-known former Bush Administration official and leading conservative advocate of sweeping executive power over national security and foreign affairs.

McCarthy also argues Hegseth should be convicted on at least one other charge:

Similarly, I do not believe there is any defending Hegseth on the charge that he has abused command authority and violated constitutional separation-of-powers principles in trying to discipline and censure Senator Kelly, a retired Navy captain (who remains subject to the Uniform Code of Military Justice). Hegseth's actions, undoubtedly endorsed by the president, constituted unlawful command influence. More importantly, they abused executive power in an effort to muffle congressional criticism. The haughty Hegseth was playing a dangerous game here; if it has now come back to bite him, he has himself to blame.

This charge is less within my expertise than some of the others. But I agree with McCarthy here.

McCarthy also appears to recognize that the Iran War is illegal, but suggests that Hegseth does not deserve impeachment on this score, because he was just obeying Trump's orders and implementing his policy. He also notes (correctly) that previous presidents have gotten away with similar initiations of war without congressional authorization.

I disagree for reasons summarized in my previous post:

Obviously, the ultimate perpetrator of these illegal acts is not Hegseth, but Trump. The former was following the latter's illegal orders (though he likely also helped influence Trump to give those orders in the first place). But sanctioning officials for obeying illegal orders is still important. That's one of the lessons of the Nuremberg trials.

I would add that Hegseth wasn't just some low-level flunky merely obeying orders. He has had a major influence on policy, and was one of the key architects of both the Iran War and the boat strikes. OK, maybe he is a flunky; but not a low-level one. He bears far greater responsibility than, e.g., servicemembers at the bottom of the chain of command.

As also noted in my earlier post, it is indeed true that previous presidents, such as Barack Obama, have gotten away with starting illegal wars. Obama deserved to be impeached, as well. But that makes it all the more imperative to start enforcing this part of the Constitution more effectively. Moreover, the Iran War is much larger and has had far worse effects than any other illegal wars of the last several decades. Obama's illegal wars were much smaller, by comparison.

I will not say much about McCarthy's analysis of the other charges, except briefly on that focused on the removal of Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro. McCarthy laments that Trump left the brutal socialist regime in power (minus Maduro), but suggests that the intervention might have been legally justified by the precedent of the 1989 US military action that removed and captured Panamanian strongman Manuel Noriega. I differ for reasons I outlined here:

Defenders of the legality of Trump's actions cite the 1989 invasion of Panama, which was undertaken in large part for the purpose of apprehending Panamian dictator Manuel Noriega; like Maduro, Noriega was charged with smuggling illegal drugs into the US. But the 1989 Panama precedent does not actually justify Trump's actions. On December 15, 1989 (five days before the US invasion), Noriega foolishly announced that Panama and the US were in a "state of war," thereby creating conflict between the two countries that did not exist in the Venezuela case. In addition, Panamanian forces had killed or wounded two US military personnel in the Panama Canal area, and detained other American citizens. Unlike Noriega in 1989, the Venezuelan regime did not declare war on the US or otherwise initiate a military conflict. Thus, congressional authorization is needed to make any US military intervention constitutional.

That said, I think the Maduro intervention charge is much weaker than the Iran War and boat strike charges. The Maduro action was on a much smaller scale, and has not had anything like the same horrific effects. The abusive prosecution charge is also more compelling than that focused on Maduro. Congress would do well to focus attention on the strongest charges and convict Hegseth on them.

“Dragon Ball Z,” a popular animation series, has musical scores written by Texas lawyer and state Sen. Nathan Johnson, D-Dallas, who was recently elected as the state’s new attorney general. (Image from Shutterstock)

Before Texas state Sen. Nathan Johnson, D-Dallas, unleashed a “blue spirit bomb” on opponent Mayes Middleton on Tuesday night in the midterm elections for the Texas attorney general spot, the Thompson Coburn lawyer composed musical scores for Dragon Ball Z, a Japanese anime series about martial artists who defend the world from destruction.

Johnson, who got at least 52% of the vote and is a Dallas lawyer, will be the first Democrat to serve as the Texas attorney general in more than 30 years, Chron.com reports.

The show introduced various terms to the United States, including “Super Saiyan,” which means getting a huge surge of physical strength and hair that stands straight up, and “blue spirit bomb,” which is something released on opponents during an attack.

A piano player, Johnson learned how to write music while working as a lawyer and liked it so much that he decided to quit his job and focus on doing film and television composition, according to the article.

Johnson eventually went back to law and started a solo practice. While looking for office space, he met a landlord connected to a Texas company that licensed the English version of Dragon Ball Z in the United States. The company then hired Johnson in the early 2000s, according to Chron.com.

“It gave me a creative outlet and a cultural connection that very few people have had the opportunity to have,” Johnson said in an interview, according to Variety.

As consumers, we create a massive amount of waste, filling up landfills with all of the products we’ve used and thrown away. While most people have a recycling bin along with their trash bin, they might not realize that many stores they frequent offer exceptional recycling programs for the items that can’t go in the recycling container.

These major retailers have robust recycling programs that can refurbish and reuse your old clothes, smartphones, rechargeable batteries, or furniture. And, for items that aren’t reusable, the retailers partner with recycling companies that can break them down into their base components to create a variety of other products.

“These sort of recycling programs are of huge importance,” says Paula Napolitano, product sales manager at Wisetek, a major Ireland-based distributor of refurbished and recycled electronics. “Last year there were around 59 million metric tons of e-waste generated globally, which is hugely impacting the environment. If large amounts of old electronics are allowed to build up in landfills, they can eventually begin to leach toxic materials into the soil, which may seriously harm the surrounding environment,” Napolitano says.

While lowering the impact you have on the local landfill is reason enough to hand off unwanted furniture, bedsheets, tablets, or rechargeable batteries to these retailers, you might be surprised to know that many of these companies offer additional incentives in the form of coupons, gift cards, and trade-in deals. Ahead, learn more about some of the top retailers who will take your unwanted stuff.

The big-box appliance and electronics giant is a leader in recycling, reusing, or repurposing, to the tune of 2.7 billion pounds of e-waste and appliances since 2009. You can drop off old electronics like computers, smartphones, radios, and more at any of Best Buy’s more than 1,000 locations and receive special promotions off certain products in the store. You can even earn gift cards for those items that still have value. Best Buy will also haul old TVs, fitness equipment, and appliances away for a nominal fee when you buy new ones.

“You can recycle up to three items per household per day,” says Alejandra Valeriano, public relations representative for Best Buy. “For $199.99, we’ll haul away and recycle up to a total of two large products (including TVs, major appliances, all-in-one computers and monitors), along with an unlimited number of select smaller products,” Valeriano says. Best Buy partners with Electronic Recyclers International, which breaks down electronics into materials that can be repurposed for use in everything from fiber optic cables to airplanes.

Few retailers have as robust a recycling program as The Home Depot. Consumers can access their comprehensive recycling web page that explains how to recycle everything from plastic plant pots to florescent tube lights. The company partners with nonprofit recycling company The Battery Network (formerly Call2Recycle) to recycle a variety of battery types, including those for power tools, EVs, and e-bikes. In 2024, The Home Depot recycled approximately 1 million pounds of rechargeable batteries. The retailer also collects plastic bags for composite manufacturer Trex, which uses them to make fencing and decking.

Not only will Staples recycle your old office supplies and electronics, they’ll pay you for it. Since 2012, Staples has recycled nearly 188 million pounds of technology. “Staples wants to make recycling easier for everyone across the U.S.,” says Mike Sauchuk, senior director of recycling and sustainability of Staples. “There are many items out there that we use every day that can be recycled, but it can be challenging to find a place to recycle them. That’s where Staples steps in. We offer free recycling for many hard-to-recycle items like technology, writing instruments, phone cases, and more. There’s no more waiting for your town’s local recycling day or event. At Staples, it’s recycling day every day.”

Through the Staples Rewards program, you can earn $5 back in rewards when you recycle tech and $2 back on every recycled ink or toner cartridge brought to one of the store’s more than 1,000 locations. In addition, the retailer will take unwanted electronics and worn-out rechargeable batteries for free.

Like other retailers, Walmart will take used cell phones, Bluetooth speakers, laptops, gaming consoles, tablets, and other devices through its trade-in program. Simply input info about the device on the Walmart website, get an offer for it, then ship it for free via FedEx or UPS Ground using a preprinted label. You receive an instant Walmart gift card for your efforts.

The presence of mercury, cadmium, lithium, and lead in car batteries ranks these vital components of cars and trucks among the more harmful products for the environment. Advance Auto Parts knows this, and therefore the company offers a nice incentive for bringing in your old battery once it dies. Take the worn-out battery to any Advance store and you’ll get a $10 gift card, which you can put toward the cost of a new battery or anything else in the store. The old batteries are then used to manufacture new ones.

While Apple’s products might be on the more expensive side when it comes to consumer electronics, they hold some of their value. That’s because the company makes it easy to cash in on that old iPhone, iPad, Macbook, or Apple Watch by allowing owners of the devices to trade their electronics in at an Apple Store or online. In return, Apple gives the customer store credit (Apple will also recycle other brands of electronics for free).

If the device is in good shape, it will be refurbished and resold. Those that can’t be reused go to one of Apple’s recycling partners, where they are broken down and recycled. Many iPhones end up with Daisy, Apple’s disassembly robot, which is designed to recover a device’s usable parts.

Habitat for Humanity’s ReStore has more than 900 locations nationwide, all of which will take appliances, furniture, various household items, and even building materials. Habitat then resells these items in its store and uses the proceeds to build affordable homes for families. “New and gently used items donated to a Habitat ReStore are resold to the community at a fraction of retail prices and help to support Habitat for Humanity’s vision of a world where everyone has a decent place to live,” says Jared Williams, communications manager at Habitat for Humanity International.

According to Williams, “Habitat ReStores tend to accept both new and gently used household items and building materials, which can include a wide variety of products.” He adds that donations come from all kinds of sources, “from neighbors completing home projects to restaurants after a remodel.” Habitat might not offer you a gift card for your stuff, but you can take tax deductions for your donations, since Habitat is a nonprofit organization.
