Ever wonder where the used products Amazon sells come from? The online retailing behemoth accepts your old electronics and devices, including Bluetooth speakers and headphones, home security devices, wireless routers, and gaming systems. The company will even reward you with gift cards for gently used electronics that it can refurbish and resell. Amazon also takes some products that are no longer functioning. The company will recycle a variety of electronic devices for free, even covering the cost of shipping them to Amazon via UPS.

Bedding, unmatched socks, old T-shirts—clothing retailer H&M will take all linens as part of the company’s recycling program. Since 2013, H&M has collected more than 172,000 tons of textiles. The items were either cleaned and reused as second-hand clothing, turned into other products such as cleaning rags, or recycled into materials like insulation. When you drop off a bag of used clothing at H&M, the company will give you a coupon toward your next purchase at their store.

More than 1 billion HP ink and toner cartridges have been recycled by customers through the company’s HP Planet Partners program. The program aims to give a second life to HP’s end-of-life equipment and printing supplies and to reduce the environmental impact of electronic waste and greenhouse gas emissions. Simply drop off your HP ink and toner supplies at a location near you, mail them back, or request a pickup if you have a large quantity of supplies to give back.

Calling all coffee enthusiasts! If you own a Nespresso machine, you might be familiar with the company’s recycling program. Fill a Nespresso recycling bag (available for free at any Nespresso store) with your used capsules and drop them off at one of the 122,000-plus collection points around the world. The aluminum from the pods is recycled into items such as bicycles, computers, and soda cans, while the used coffee grounds create compost or green energy.

Kroger recognizes that most shoppers throw out plastic grocery bags and packaging after shopping, so they’ve put a special system in place for customers to take your discarded grocery bags and packaging and recycle them responsibly. The retail giant provides convenient drop-off bins to recycle plastic. The grocery chain has recycled more than 180 million pounds of plastic and aims to eliminate single-use plastic grocery bags in all of their stores by 2025.

Williams-Sonoma has a variety of initiatives dedicated to creating a more circular economy. The company works with donation programs like Good360 to give away returned and unsold products to local nonprofit organizations and others. They are also exploring rental and resale business models to give a second life to products like bedding, curtains, throws, pillows, linens, and more.

#7711. 5 Smart Tips for Soundproofing Windows

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Gretchen Heber, Bob Vila, Manasa Reddigari

Updated Nov 10, 2026 12:27 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Whether it’s highway traffic, loud neighbors, or birds chirping, if you don’t have sound proof windows, some noise from the outside world is bound to disrupt your daily activities, especially if the racket intrudes when you’re in a bedroom or other area intended as a sanctuary or work space. While you can’t control what goes on outside, you can block (or at least reduce) the noise by soundproofing windows using these techniques. Whether you implement one of these strategies or a combination thereof, you may find that soundproofing windows is your secret to attaining inner peace.

Soundproofing windows in your home can help you dampen noise for better sleep, and block out ambient noise in your home office. Window inserts are probably the most effective options, but they are expensive—they’ll set you back $300 to $800 per insert. Replacing older single-pane windows with updated double-pane windows, which cost $350 to $900 (and sometimes more) is another effective solution, albeit another big investment. A more affordable way to soundproof windows is to seal window gaps with acoustic caulk, which costs just $10 to $20. Sound-reducing window treatments, which start at about $20 each, are another cost-effective way to go.

If you live in an environment with heavy noise pollution, such as honking car horns, wailing sirens, or music blasting from next door, utilizing soundproofing window inserts is the most effective way to reduce the cacophony. These glass inserts are installed in the window frame a few inches in front of the interior face of your existing window. The air space between the insert and the window keeps most sound vibrations from passing through the glass, resulting in greater noise-reduction benefits than double-pane windows alone (more on these ahead). The most effective inserts are made of laminated glass, a thick glass consisting of two layers of glass with an intervening layer of plastic that effectively blocks vibrations. Some companies that make these inserts include Indow, Soundproof Windows, and CitiQuiet.

On the Sound Transmission Class (STC) scale that reflects the decibel reduction in noise volume that a window provides, soundproof windows typically measure between 48 and 54—the higher the STC, the greater the noise-reduction benefit. At the upper end, this means that a 98-decibel (db) outside noise (e.g., a motorcycle engine) is heard at only 44 db indoors (98 minus 54), which is no louder than a typical indoor conversation. You’ll get more noise reduction benefits by installing an insert in front of a single-pane window than you would with a double-pane window. This is because the STC of a double-pane window is often higher to begin with, so an insert won’t increase its overall STC as substantially. An insert for one window typically costs between $350 and $800 installed, which is less than or equal to the cost of the next option for soundproofing windows: a window replacement.

If you experience moderate outdoor noise pollution, such as the occasional lawn mower or a passing car, you may wish to replace single-pane windows with double-pane windows. Single-pane pane windows, often found in homes 15 years old or older, have just a single piece of glass in the window frame, while double-pane windows, the standard in newer homes, consist of two pieces of glass with air between them. Single-pane windows provide no air barrier between the outside and the glass, so they permit virtually all outdoor sounds to vibrate through the glass, resulting in a noisy interior.

Single-pane windows have an STC of between 26 and 28, which is only a little over half that of soundproof windows. At the upper end of this range, the window would reduce the noise volume of a passing car (70 db) to 42 db (70 minus 28). In contrast, the air space between the individual panes of a double-pane window helps halt the vibration of outdoor sounds through the glass, resulting in greater noise reduction benefit translating to an STC of 26 to 35. Compared with a single-pane window with an STC of 28, a double-pane window measuring in at 35 would reduce the noise volume of a passing car to only 35 db—offering a 7-decibel greater reduction in noise than the single-pane window (70 minus 35). While this may not seem like much, to the listener, a 7-db difference results in a perceived volume reduction of around 87 percent. Replacing one single-pane window with a double-pane equivalent will run you $350 to $900.

RELATED: Soundproofing a Room: The Two Best Ways to Dampen Noise Without Tearing Down Your Walls

Small gaps between a window frame and an interior wall can let outdoor noise into your home and keep your windows from performing at their STC rating. A simple way to seal these gaps is to fill them with an acoustic caulk, such as Green Glue Acoustical Caulk. This noiseproof, latex-based product reduces sound transmission and maintains windows’ STC but still allows you to open and close the windows.

Applying acoustic caulk is the easiest and most inexpensive way to soundproof windows. If there is already silicone caulk around the window frame, remove it with a putty knife. Cut a quarter-inch opening in the tip of the acoustic caulk tube with a utility knife, load the tube into a caulking gun, and pull the gun’s trigger to apply a thin bead of caulk in the gap between the interior window frame and interior wall.

Acoustic caulk readily bonds with most window frame and wall materials, including wood and drywall. More flexible than regular silicone caulk, acoustic caulk won’t shrink or form new cracks over time as you operate your windows; it’s also ultra-durable, lasting for several years before it requires re-caulking. Though you’ll most often find it white, acoustic caulk is available in a variety of hues. Some products turn clear as they dry, while others remain their original color but can be painted to match the color of interior walls.

To soften noise as well as reduce harsh glare, hang sound-dampening curtains. PONY DANCE’s blackout curtains, which were the top overall pick in our tested guide to the best soundproof curtains, are a top-quality option. Sound-dampening curtains, which usually cost $20 to $60 per panel, are made of a thick, heavy fabric such as velvet, and are typically lined with vinyl or a similar material that absorbs sound. These curtains also minimize echoes. Because they dampen but do not block sound entirely, they’re better suited for light noise pollution that may interrupt sleep, such as crickets or birds chirping, than they are for dampening the sound of heavy street traffic.

Many of these window treatments also serve as quality blackout curtains, which have a foam backing that helps block out light. Curtains that absorb sound and block light are great options for soundproofing bedrooms and other spaces designed for sleep and relaxation. They are especially popular with people who work night-shift hours and sleep during the day.

These lightweight linen blackout curtains reduced sound by 5 decibels in our hands-on testing. See our full review.

Cellular shades, also known as honeycomb shades, consist of rows of cells or hexagonal tubes of fabric stacked on top of each other. These shades serve several purposes: They block out light, prevent indoor heat gain in the summer and retain heat in winter, and absorb sound that vibrates into a room to reduce the echo. While single-cell shades have a single layer of cells and absorb limited sound, double-cell shades (such as those by First Rate Blinds) have two layers of cells and thus absorb more sound. Like sound-dampening curtains, they’re best suited for people who experience low levels of noise pollution.

Whether you live in an urban apartment where the noise of blaring horns is enough to drive you mad, or in a rural neighborhood where early-rising roosters create a cacophony, sometimes you just need relief from the racket. Addressing deficiencies in your windows’ soundproofing is one way to do that.

You may elect to replace your windows altogether, or you might choose to layer in some sound-blocking elements. Either way, relief from exterior racket isn’t too difficult to find. As for that drum kit your in-laws bought for the kids, you’re on your own there, though soundproofing your doors might be a good start.

The most affordable way to soundproof your windows is to caulk them with acoustic caulk. Remove any existing silicone caulk and recaulk with a product that is specifically designed to block window noise. A tube of acoustic caulk costs about $20. Window treatments are another economical way to soundproof your windows.

If you have single-pane windows or have no soundproofing materials in place, the sound of the wind blowing through the trees may be loud enough to permeate the windows. Or, you could be hearing wind whistling into the house, entering through gaps between window sashes and other parts of the window housing, such as the sill, jambs, or casing.

You can’t purchase 100 percent soundproof windows; they don’t exist. Noise-reduction windows can block up to 90 to 95 percent of sound.

Curb Appeal Updates You’ll Appreciate Even If You Aren’t Selling Your Home

Curb appeal does not have to be solely cosmetic. See which good-looking projects we are prioritizing to make homes safer, more energy-efficient, and weather resistant.

#7710. How to Use an Axe Safely

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 10, 2026 1:29 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Ever since someone put a club and stone together to make the first axe, it has remained a handy tool that has made life easier. Sure, you could fire up a chainsaw to do many things that an axe can do — like chopping wood for fuel, creating wood sculptures, prepping building materials, and clearing land, but an axe doesn’t require any fuel, is way easier to transport, and quieter.

While it may be one of the original tools that humans used, it’s still a tool that comes with risks and it’s important to know how to use an axe safely. It’s also crucial to know the differences among the various axes so you know which one will best suit your needs and how to use it safely and with the right technique.

It’s helpful to know the names for the main parts of an axe so that it’s easier to compare various models, and decide which type is right for your needs. Here are some key axe parts:

It’s not hard to imagine how things can go really wrong when using an axe. In addition to practicing with the axe so you feel confident using it, there are guidelines you should follow to stay safe.

While it may seem like power is the most important part of successful axe-swinging, control and technique have greater influence on success. Even though the weight of the axe helps increase the force, trying to swing an axe that’s too heavy for your abilities is never a good idea. You’ll have better success if you reach for an axe that’s a comfortable weight.

No matter the task, the technique for using an axe is similar.

Most felling strokes are diagonal, but some are horizontal to create a notch in the tree so it will fall. Always position your body (or halt your swing) so that the follow-through does not hit your body. And never stand in the path of where the tree may fall.

The Fiskars X27 is 36 inches long and weighs 6.3 pounds; requires strength to wield but cuts decisively. Read the review.

Limbing can be more dangerous than felling because you are dealing with smaller pieces and a great deal of sharp force near your body. Often, limbing happens while you are standing on a fallen tree. But if you aren’t, make sure there is ample distance between you and the arc of the axe swing. It’s usually easiest to start at the bottom of the tree and work your way to the top branches, swinging in the direction of the top of the tree as you go.

After a downed tree is limbed, it’s ready to be bucked into transportable lengths. Make sure the log won’t roll before you begin. Then, stand on the log and strike the axe below and between your feet.

Cutting logs along the grain is called splitting. A split log dries out faster, and will be ready quicker for a fireplace or fire pit. After placing a log vertically on a chopping block, aim at the face and swing the axe to make contact.

A competitive activity that’s become popular in recent years, axe throwing is usually done in a controlled space. While standing with your nondominant leg forward and at least 12 feet away from the target, pull the axe back over your head. With arms slightly bent, release the axe forward. Just like in golf, follow-through is essential.

Your axe will stay in great shape for a long time with proper care and maintenance. It only takes a few minutes after each use to keep it in fine shape. Plus, it will benefit from oiling and sharpening once a year.

Safely using an axe depends on careful planning about where and when you use the tool. It’s essential to select the right axe based on the task. And it takes practice to know how to hold an axe and how to swing an axe with ease. Never attempt to swing an axe if you feel nervous, if it’s dark out, or if people or pets are within your swing zone.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

The main advantage of this type of heater is that it doesn’t take up any valuable floor space, which is important in small bathrooms. It has a modern, slim look with air inlet on the sides to hide internal mechanical parts, not to mention an impact-resistant façade that makes it a safe and sustainable choice. The unit is compact but still has strong performance, from 1,000 to 1,500 watts of heating power, depending on the model.

This heating unit is known for optimal comfort and ease of use. It contains an element that produces instant heat, while the exceptionally quiet fan ensures a quick rise in temperature. In addition, hot air flows out from the bottom of the unit to provide good heat distribution throughout the room. You can choose a model to be paired with a wall thermostat or one with a two-button built-in electronic thermostat to increase energy savings. Finally, Stelpro’s fan heaters can be used to retrofit most competitors’ units.

Ideal for bathrooms, the Sonoma Style fan heater is the new standard for those who need a quiet but fast heating solution.

If you use your garage for more than just parking cars—such as for a workshop or gym—then it’s important to keep the temperature comfortable, no matter how cold it gets outside. Garages aren’t designed to stay warm, as they typically have bare concrete floors and lack insulation. By installing a special type of heater made for garages, you can continue using this space throughout the colder months. Plus, it will protect your tools, paint, and other home supplies from getting ruined by being stored in icy temperatures.

Even if you try running a portable space heater, the temperature inside the garage probably won’t rise more than a few degrees. That’s why installing an electric heating unit like Stelpro’s Spider Ceiling Fan Heater is the best way to ensure you can continue using your garage all year long. Designed specifically for residential garage environments, the Spider’s combination of optimal performance, instant heat using 4,000W of heating power, quiet operation, and stylish red and stainless steel finishes will be a great addition to any garage.

The Spider heater is purposely compact and mounts on the ceiling, so it can heat the entire garage without taking up valuable floor or wall space that you can instead use to hang tools, bicycles, and other garage-friendly items. Finally, you’ll be able to conveniently control this heater using an electronic wall thermostat (not included).

Designed specifically for garage environments, the Spider’s combination of optimal performance, instant heat, and distinct design are a surefire hit.

Ready to modernize your home heating system? Explore Stelpro’s latest offerings that blend performance with style.

#7706. The Best Gifts for Pros, From Electricians to Carpenters: 32 Tools and Gear They’ll Actually Use

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 10, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Professionals in any industry need tools and supplies they can rely on to get the job done. If you have a pro in your household, family, or friend group, then they are sure to appreciate pro-grade gifts for birthdays, holidays, and any other special occasions on the horizon. Whether you are looking for tools, like the best paint sprayers, or products, like gutter sealant and stain, you will find a variety of the best gifts for the pros in your life below.

Anyone who hauls tools from the truck to the jobsite will appreciate a box that’s built to take the abuse. The Milwaukee Packout Large Tool Box earned our Best Weather-Rated pick in our guide to the best tool boxes for its rugged, watertight build and latches that open with one hand. It also stacks, rolls, and locks together with other Packout boxes, so it’s an easy gift for a pro who already uses the system or wants to start one.

What our tester says: “Although the box features steel latches that hold the top down securely, we were able to open and latch them with one hand. The Milwaukee tool box comes with a 100-pound weight limit and we have no reason to doubt that. We loaded it with heavy tools and sockets and even overloaded it a bit so we had to push the lid to get it to close. The latches (and hinges) held tight.” —Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Milwaukee tool box at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Ace Hardware.

Electricians spend their days on ladders, in attics and crawl spaces, and on uneven ground, so supportive, dry feet make a real difference. The Ariat Rebar Wedge Chelsea Work Boot offers ergonomic support, even on rough terrain, and a breathable waterproof construction that keeps feet dry in rain or snow. The pull-on style is easy to slip on and off between jobs. If the recipient needs electrical hazard-rated footwear, check the listing for that rating before ordering.

Get the Rebar Wedge Chelsea Work Boot at Ariat or Amazon.

Hearing protection is a practical gift for any pro who spends the day around loud tools, and this one makes long days more enjoyable. The 3M WorkTunes Connect has a 26 dB NRR, which is suitable for mowing, and it pairs with a phone to stream music or podcasts and take calls. It combines hearing protection and headphones in one headset, so a pro can protect their hearing without giving up the playlist. 3M’s WorkTunes line was our Best Bluetooth pick in our guide to the best hearing protection.

What our tester says: “The audio quality was really good for both music and conversation, and the microphone did a great job of filtering out mower noise during phone calls. As for comfort, the WorkTunes headphones totally outclassed Bluetooth earbuds.” —Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the 3M WorkTunes Connect hearing protector at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

A hard hat gets worn all day, so comfort matters as much as protection, and that’s what makes this Milwaukee helmet a thoughtful gift. It has a vented shell to help reduce heat, a 5-point adjustable chin strap, and a headlamp mount for dim spaces. The machine-washable antimicrobial sweatband and liner are easy to keep fresh, which makes it a safety upgrade a pro will actually notice. It was our Best Overall pick in our guide to the best hard hats.

What our tester says: “The Milwaukee Bolt Vented Safety Helmet stands out for its combination of high-level protection, comfort, and smart accessory compatibility. Unlike standard hard hats, this helmet provides both top and side impact protection, meeting ANSI Type 2 standards as well as European EN12492 climbing helmet requirements.” —Paul Rankin, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Milwaukee Bolt safety helmet at The Home Depot or Ace Hardware (in black).

Framers and carpenters carry their fasteners and tools on their body all day, so a well-made tool belt is a gift they’ll use constantly. This Occidental Leather set includes a heavy-duty belt, a hammer loop, and two bags with plenty of tool pockets. The bags slide along the belt for an adjustable fit, and the set comes in various sizes, so check the recipient’s size before ordering. Occidental Leather’s framer sets are featured in our guide to the best framing tool belts.

What our tester says: “With its thick material and ample stitching and rivets, we found that there was no doubt about this belt’s quality and durability. The belt itself was comfortable and distributed weight nicely, and since it tapers at the front, it’s comfortable when bending forward. Being able to slide the bags around on the belt was also a big part of that.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Occidental leather tool belt at Amazon.

Small enough to slip into a stocking or slide beneath a big bow, the WD-40 Precision Pen is perfect for adding a bit of lubricant exactly where it’s needed. But that precision doesn’t come from its overall size, it comes from the fine-point felt tip that applies a single drop without overspray. And with a rubberized grip for comfort and a leak-resistant cap for safe carrying, it’s just as easy to use as it is to toss in a pocket or toolbox.

Read our full review: WD-40 Precision Pen

Electricians test the current before and after working on a system, so a dependable clamp meter is a gift they’ll reach for on nearly every job. The Klein Tools CL390 has a side-mounted trigger that opens the jaws to test one conductor at a time, plus a jaw-mounted noncontact tester on the end. The kit includes standard leads for amperage, voltage, resistance, duty cycle, capacitance, and diode testing, so it covers the checks a pro does most. It was our Best Clamp pick in our guide to the best multimeters.

What our tester says: “This clamp meter proved to be pretty convenient. Accuracy matters on a jobsite, where a measurement that’s off by a few inches can mean recutting and reassembling pieces. Get the Bosch Blaze laser measure at Amazon or The Home Depot.

A pipe wrench is a plumber’s everyday tool, and this Milwaukee Cheater is a step up from the basic wrench most already own. #7705. New Mexico Supreme Court permanently disbars prosecutor after disciplinary findings

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials.

Cosme Ripol, a prosecutor from the district attorney’s office for the Eighth Judicial District in Taos, New Mexico, was disbarred Monday, effective immediately.

All five justices on the state supreme court agreed on the disciplinary board’s recommendation. The proceedings focused on three criminal cases that Ripol prosecuted between 2022 and 2024.

According to coverage by the Santa Fe New Mexican, a pivotal case in the investigation was State v. Desiree Lensegrav, where the defendant was convicted in 2022 of first-degree murder, kidnapping, conspiracy and tampering with evidence.

The New Mexico Supreme Court vacated Lensegrav’s convictions after it learned that Ripol, who had been licensed to practice law in the state since 1986, used inadmissible evidence and made derogatory statements about the defendant during the trial.

“As the supreme court noted, prosecutors are held to a higher standard because of their unique responsibility to seek justice,” said Marcus Montoya, the district attorney for the Eighth Judicial District, in a statement Monday. “When improper tactics are employed in the courtroom, even by an attorney with more than 30 years of criminal law experience, that standard is not met.”

#7700. Disability Discrimination and Allegations of AI Use in Student's University of Michigan Course Papers

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"[A]t this stage of the case, ... [plaintiff] plausibly pleads that [the university] discriminated against her by disregarding [her medial records] to find that she used AI when the writing style of the course papers could have resulted from her disabilities."

From Doe v. Regents of Univ. of Mich., decided yesterday by Judge Laurie J. Michelson (E.D. Mich.):

Plaintiff Jane Doe filed this lawsuit against the University of Michigan and several individual defendants after she was disciplined for her alleged use of AI to write course papers. Plaintiff, who has generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), maintains that the "tone, meticulous structure, [and] stylistic consistency" of her writing can be misinterpreted as AI. Unconvinced, Defendants sanctioned Plaintiff with disciplinary probation and required her to rewrite those course papers and write a reflective essay. After challenging that discipline without success, Plaintiff filed suit, asserting claims under the due process clause, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and the Rehabilitation Act (RA). …

This dispute unfolded last fall when Plaintiff was an undergraduate student in Great Books 191, a classical studies course at the University of Michigan. The class was taught by Theo Nash, the course's graduate student instructor, and Basil Duffalo, the lead instructor. According to Plaintiff, Nash made public "statements reflecting a predisposition to assume AI misuse by students and to treat AI-related concerns as a core academic 'values' issue."

The issues at the heart of this case started when Nash filed an academic misconduct accusation with the Office of Student Academic Affairs (OSAA), indicating he was "immediately suspicious" Plaintiff had used AI to write a course paper. Plaintiff denied that accusation, "explaining that [her] disability-related writing traits could be misinterpreted as AI and should not be treated as proof of misconduct."

Plaintiff participated in a conference with OSAA and submitted materials supporting that position. Not long after, Nash filed a second misconduct accusation based on another paper written by Plaintiff. He attached "AI-generated comparison outputs created by prompting AI with [Plaintiff's] own outline and with instructor feedback." Before OSAA's involvement on this second accusation, Nash asked Plaintiff to meet. Plaintiff declined. In Plaintiff's telling, Nash "interpreted her declination as 'self-destructive' and a refusal of help." Plaintiff then went through the same OSAA proceeding for the second accusation. OSAA found Plaintiff responsible for both accusations and sanctioned her with disciplinary probation (notated on her unofficial transcript) and also required her to write a reflective essay.

Five days later, Nash filed a third misconduct accusation with OSAA for another paper written by Plaintiff. Plaintiff again submitted materials to OSAA including "written notices" "explaining that an NR grade was blocking degree requirements and graduation and that her transcript and future educational opportunities were being harmed immediately."

Before OSAA adjudicated the third accusation, Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Dean of the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, and the University President's Office, "about disability discrimination, retaliation, harassment, and lack of procedural neutrality in the OSAA process." The University responded that Plaintiff could appeal OSAA's findings, which Plaintiff soon did. That same day, Plaintiff filed a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education and the University's Equity, Civil Rights, and Title IX Office (ECRT). OSAA, in turn, paused Plaintiff's appeal pending ECRT's review.

ECRT dismissed Plaintiff's complaint given her approved accommodations. With that decision complete, OSAA then issued the same misconduct finding for the third accusation. Plaintiff was also required to rewrite course papers for Great Books 191.

In Plaintiff's view, Defendants "treated disability-related traits and limitations as evidence of guilt and failed to apply disability-informed modifications in the academic integrity process." That led Plaintiff to file this lawsuit. Plaintiff brings her claims against the Regents of the University of Michigan ("the University") and several individual defendants in their official and individual capacities, including Nash and Duffalo, and Sean Edgerton and Christine O'Neil from OSAA. …

The court held the individual defendants were entitled to qualified immunity as to the due process claim, since any alleged constitutional violation wouldn't be "clear to a reasonable" government official; an excerpt:

Based on the allegations in the complaint, Nash (and Duffalo) were faced with course papers that resembled the use of AI. Plaintiff has provided no case suggesting it would be "clear to a reasonable" university instructor that using AI-detection software to analyze that writing and bring an academic misconduct allegation as a result of that analysis would violate a student's procedural due process rights….

And the court rejected the due process claim against the institution:

[Plaintiff] was advised of the accusations that she used AI to write course papers. Her sanctions included disciplinary probation notated on her unofficial transcript, a requirement to write a reflective essay, and rewriting course papers. But before they were imposed, Plaintiff was given opportunities to provide her side of the story, including that her GAD and OCD caused writing traits that could be mistaken for AI. She provided medical documentation to OSAA, and OSAA expressly considered that information in its decision. In effect, Plaintiff "admits that [s]he received exactly the due process [s]he requested."

Pivoting from the process provided, Plaintiff maintains that OSAA's sanctions "rested on Nash's self-confirming AI comparison outputs." That argument is unsupported by Plaintiff's allegations and exhibits. Again, they show that OSAA considered Nash's conclusions against Plaintiff's explanations. And when forming its decision, OSAA even credited information Plaintiff provided that sufficiently disputed one of Nash's conclusions … ("In your evidence you indicated that the idea of the 'rat king' was something talked about in your discussion section which we were able to confirm.")….

All told, "[w]hen assessing whether an academic dismissal constituted a due process violation, '[a] court must 'show great respect for the faculty's professional judgment' and may not 'override' that judgment 'unless it is such a substantial departure from accepted academic norms as to demonstrate that the … committee responsible did not actually exercise professional judgment.'" The parties rely on this academic-dismissal standard even though this case involves assessing whether a disciplinary probation notation on an unofficial transcript and a requirement to write a reflective essay and rewrite course papers constitute a due process violation. But based on the allegations in the complaint and attached exhibits, the Court cannot find that Defendants departed from accepted academic norms or failed to exercise professional judgment.

The court also rejected plaintiff's claims that the university failed to accommodate her disability, and that the university retaliated against her for asserting rights related to her disability. But it allowed plaintiff's intentional disability discrimination claim to go forward:

[Plaintiff] describes the discrimination theory in her response brief as follows:

Nash's public statements reflecting a 'paranoid' predisposition to find AI everywhere, combined with his decision to file three successive accusations grounded in the very writing traits Plaintiff's clinicians had warned would be misinterpreted, and OSAA's decision to sustain those findings while disregarding the clinical record, collectively support an inference of intentional discrimination.

For their part, Defendants do not advance significant argument on this claim[, arguing instead that] … "With respect to the denominated claims of 'discrimination,' the Complaint does not actually contain any allegations of direct (i.e., intentional) discrimination. For that reason and to that extent, Claims I and II should be dismissed." … Yet Plaintiff maintains that her discrimination claims "are supported by allegations of intentional … discrimination." …

There can be no dispute that Plaintiff pleads Nash's "paranoid' predisposition" to find AI, and her submission of clinical evidence explaining why, given her disabilities, her writing style might be misinterpreted as coming from the use of AI. It is also true that the exhibits Plaintiff attached to her response brief that the parties are treating as integral to the allegations in the complaint, show that OSAA reviewed her clinical record.

But at this stage of the case, the Court must accept as true Plaintiff's allegation that OSAA disregarded the medical evidence. In other words, although Defendants considered and/or reviewed Plaintiff's medical records, she plausibly pleads that they discriminated against her by disregarding them to find that she used AI when the writing style of the course papers could have resulted from her disabilities.

Plaintiff further alleges that she provided Nash and Duffalo with information about her disability accommodations such that they were on notice of her disabilities. She pleads that she rejected Nash's request to meet with him outside of OSAA. Taking these allegations as true and drawing reasonable inferences in Plaintiff's favor, that rejection likely resulted from the effects of her disabilities, including difficulty with "live verbal defense, rapid processing, and adversarial questioning."

Indeed, that is seemingly why "Plaintiff requested that OSAA permit her to present her defenses in writing rather than through additional live Zoom proceedings, consistent with her disability-related limitations." But Nash, according to the allegations, interpreted Plaintiff's rejection of his request to meet as "self-destructive" and then followed up with another misconduct accusation to OSAA. Accepting these allegations as true, combined with Plaintiff's allegations about Nash's "'paranoid' predisposition" to find AI, Plaintiff plausibly pleads a claim for disability discrimination under the ADA/RA.

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 10, 1975

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Hydroponic systems, which allow plants to grow in water rather than soil, are popular because they offer a way to produce a bounty of plants in a relatively small area in an indoor garden. These systems also tend to be user-friendly, so even newbie growers are likely to succeed. We recently tested eight popular models, spending several months setting them up and evaluating their various features while growing a range of plants.

We also evaluated each tested hydroponics system for its ease of use, value, functionality, appearance, and build quality. With these factors in mind, our favorite is Ahopegarden’s 10-Pod Aeroponics Growing Kit. It offers the flexibility to grow almost any type of plant, is easy to set up, and provides a good value for the money.

But Ahopegarden isn’t the only show in town. Some of the other kits we tested also ranked highly and may better fit your indoor gardening needs depending on the available space and desired setup. Check out our top picks of some of the best hydroponic systems to get started.

Bottom line: Explore the best hydroponic systems of 2026, from compact kits to large setups, each offering unique features for indoor gardening success.

To qualify as one of our top picks, we required each hydroponic system to have a water circulation system to keep the water fresh. When evaluating all-inclusive systems, we looked for bright grow lights that could be adjusted in height as the plants grow taller. The following hydroponic systems vary in design and size, but each is well suited to growing healthy herbs and plants indoors.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 5/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 5/5

The Ahopegarden offers an affordable way to grow fruits, vegetables, or flowers at home. It has the capacity to grow 10 plants and comes with baskets, sponges, plant food, and grow domes—everything needed to get started except for seeds. While this system can be used to produce any type of plant, the adjustable light reaches a maximum height of 14.6 inches, so users will need to select plant varieties that won’t exceed this.

We chose a dwarf tomato variety and mini bell pepper to grow in our Ahopegarden, planting five of each seed. Setting the system up required us to soak the sponges, fill the water tank, and use tweezers to add 2 to 3 seeds to each sponge (some larger seeds must be soaked for 6 to 12 hours before planting). We added grow domes to our plant pods and selected the “vegetable” button on the top of the light panel, which put the grow light on the appropriate timer.

We love this system’s flexibility. It’s also on the smaller side, so it’s easy to find a spot for it, even in cramped spaces. Our biggest concern is that there isn’t much spacing between the pods, so depending on the plant, it can get crowded.

What our tester says: “The Ahopegarden was simple to set up. We love that it has automatic lights for growing fruits and flowers or vegetables. We planted dwarf tomatoes and mini bell peppers in our growing kit, and they sprouted within a week.”—Katie Barton, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Ahopegarden hydroponic system at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 4/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 4/5

The AeroGarden Bounty grows up to nine plants and comes with a seed kit of the user’s choice. Thanks to a convenient touch screen, growers can easily set their own light and watering schedule, and there’s a vacation mode for when the system will be unattended.

One of the system’s best features is its tall grow height of 24 inches—the highest of any smaller hydroponic system in our lineup. The grow height makes it easier to nurture larger plant varieties, such as peppers and tomatoes, without worrying about plants getting their leaves singed on the lights. The system also includes a trellis, which is helpful when growing such larger plants.

The Bounty has a large water reservoir, so the system needs minimal topping off. It also comes with liquid plant food and humidity caps for seeds to germinate. However, in testing—growing a combination of lettuces and herbs—the width of the system proved a bit short. This led to stunted growth of some plants, while others competed for light. For example, when we placed cilantro and a short lettuce variety next to each other, the cilantro grew taller and blocked light from the lettuce, which failed to truly thrive.

While AeroGarden could fix this problem by making the Bounty wider, we found the solution to be simply using fewer grow stations simultaneously. When replanting seeds in the system during a second round of testing, we planted fewer plants (six instead of nine) and found that they did better, growing larger and looking healthier.

What our tester says: “Despite the width of the system being a bit short for my preferences, after I figured out how to work around this issue, the AeroGarden Bounty earned one of the best overall spots for the number of plants it grows, its reasonable price, its tall grow height, and for being an inclusive kit that makes hydroponics simple.”—Jenn Ryan, Product Reviews tester and writer

While the system doesn’t include LED lights or a water-recirculating pump, it works via a tried-and-true plant-propagation method that is simple but effective. When roots develop, plants can be transplanted into pots or to an outdoor garden spot.

During testing, we found this system was very easy to set up. We also appreciated its small size and good looks; it could beautify just about any spot that gets enough natural light for plants. However, we found the necks of the glass vases to be quite narrow—while we could easily fit herbs (such as the rosemary we rooted), we had trouble getting snake plants and succulents into the water. That issue aside, this system gets high marks for its affordability, attractiveness, simple setup, and effectiveness in helping plants grow roots.

The Lettuce Grow Farmstand has the capacity for 36 full-size plants, making it the largest hydroponic system on our list. It comes with a teardrop-shaped base that can hold 20 gallons of water, which means we didn’t have to top off the water reservoir as often as with some of the smaller systems.

The Click & Grow is an attractive indoor garden ideal for beginners or those with limited space. It comes with everything a user needs to get started, including plant pods, grow domes, and easy-to-follow instructions.

Plantaform’s Smart Indoor Garden is a fogponics system that turns a fertilizer and water mixture into fog, delivering nutrients to the plant’s root system. It comes with 15 pods, a lettuce mix plant pack, germination domes, and plant food. Six other plant pack varieties are available for purchase separately.

When we received the Plantaform grow kit, we were impressed by its quality, futuristic look. Get the Plantaform hydroponics system at Plantaform.

When evaluating these hydroponic home garden systems, we considered over a dozen companies and looked at the brand, customer reviews, features of the product, extra items included, and how well the system grew plants. We also looked at durability and ease of use when testing and evaluating these products.

We scored each product using a rubric that evaluated the watering system, how well the plants in the system thrived, how easy the system was to set up and use, any extra features the product included, types of plants the system could grow, the durability of the product, and how attractive the setup was. We also considered the cost value of each product.

As we tested each hydroponic system, we looked closely at how well the plants grew and how easy the system was to use and maintain. To do this, we tested each system for a minimum of a month, and some of the systems were tested for over a year.

Plants need four essential elements to thrive: water, oxygen, light, and nutrients. A successful hydroponic system must supply an adequate amount of all four. For those new to cultivating an indoor garden, the options may seem confusing, but today’s manufacturers offer various types of hydroponic systems that automate much of the process.

While all hydroponic systems supply plant roots with water and nutrients, the method varies. There are six common types of hydroponic systems, all with unique strong points, but some are better suited to commercial settings than DIY home settings.

Hydroponic gardening at home is not difficult, but the operator will need basic knowledge about how hydroponics work. This means, for most systems, that growers should have some experience in sprouting plants from seeds, knowing when plants need plant food, monitoring the water flow of the reservoir, and adjusting nutrient levels and pH.

Fortunately, with today’s consumer hydroponic systems, indoor gardening is simple and straightforward. Systems like the popular AeroGarden come with mesh pods and soilless medium (often coconut coir plugs), as well as a pump for circulating water and keeping roots moist and healthy. Unlike classic terrariums, most of today’s in-home systems also feature grow lights on timers that provide the correct amount of light for optimal growth.

One of the convenient characteristics of a hydroponic grow system is that users can grow more plants in less space because the roots don’t need to spread out to seek nutrients. Depending on the type of setup, hydroponic systems can be as small as a few inches deep by a few inches wide or as big as a few feet deep by a few feet wide. The most common models, such as the AeroGarden Harvest, can fit on a kitchen countertop, ladder plant stand, or a table and take up no more than 1 to 2 square feet of space—yet some models can grow up to 30 full-size plants.

Indoor hydroponic systems can grow a wide variety of plant types. While smaller systems, such as the AeroGarden, are best used for herbs and smaller varieties of peppers and tomatoes, larger systems like the Lettuce Grow Farmstand can grow virtually anything, including large lettuces, full-size tomato or pepper plants, kale, Swiss chard, bok choy, and even cabbage. Flowers can be grown in hydroponic systems, too.

Consistent temperature is essential to plant growth, so commercial hydroponic growers often have water heaters to regulate the water temperature. However, in-home hydroponic systems don’t require the same temperature-control level because they’re usually placed in a home where the temperature remains between 60 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Many experts suggest that the optimal water temperature for plant growth is between 68 and 71.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

Unlike self-watering planter systems, a soilless growing medium is normally used in hydroponic gardening. These mediums can include coconut coir plugs or mineral wool. However, some systems, such as the Lettuce Grow Farmstand, have plants that are started in actual soil and then transplanted into small pods to grow without additional soil in the hydroponic system.

Some systems come with plants or seeds already in the substrate. As the plants grow, the roots extend below the pod into the reservoir or channel beneath.

Nutrients used in hydroponic systems can be in either powder or liquid form. Some come with powders that must be dissolved in warm water before being added to the water reservoir, while other systems come with liquid plant food that can be poured directly into the reservoir.

Automated hydroponic systems require minimal maintenance relative to a traditional garden or a DIY hydroponics system. Most systems recommend topping off the tank reservoir about once a week and adding plant food at the same time. It’s also recommended that the reservoir be cleaned every month or so to prevent the buildup of algae in the tank.

During the growing cycle, users may also need to wipe down the unit’s surface with a clean, damp rag to maintain its appearance—they aren’t immune to dust!

There are many advantages to owning a hydroponic grow kit, including water conservation, reduced risk of pest problems, and fresh produce year-round.

According to Dr. Michael B. Timmons, professor emeritus and graduate professor in the Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering at Cornell University, “Producing food as efficiently as possible and minimizing the use of our scarce resources should be a goal for everyone. Each family could contribute toward this goal by choosing to produce some or all of the vegetables they eat. Producing vegetables hydroponically using controlled environment agriculture (CEA) … uses 90 percent less water and land than conventional agriculture.” He goes on to say that those who grow some of their food hydroponically can reduce the associated carbon footprint by producing in their own home, garage, or mini-greenhouse.

As explained by the Oklahoma State University Extension, one of the advantages of utilizing a hydroponic system to grow vegetables and flowers is being able to control the nutrients and growing environment. Hydroponic systems also reduce the risk of chemical exposure due to pesticides as well as the risk of pests infesting the plants and soil (although the plants are not immune to pests that may travel indoors). Finally, with an all-inclusive hydroponic system, growing herbs, fruits, veggies, or flowers indoors needn’t take a lot of time or require a large garden or a sunny window.

Because hydroponic systems automate the growing process, users don’t need a lot of gardening or hydroponic knowledge to enjoy fresh herbs and produce. For those new to growing indoors, however, some questions are to be expected. Read on for answers that provide basic info.

For those just developing a green thumb, an affordable hydroponics system that automates lighting and watering and provides a few growing stations is ideal.

Most systems come with built-in aeration via a pump, so additional aeration is not needed.

No. Nutrient solutions are preformulated to offer the best pH level for a wide variety of plants and herbs. However, you may want to test the pH level of the water in the reservoir with a pH test kit and add pH-adjusting liquid to raise or lower the pH level to about 6 or 7, which is the ideal range for growing vegetables and herbs.

To maintain a strict pH level, pH-adjusting liquids are available, and a couple of drops of either “pH Up” or “pH Down” can change the level. Some hydroponic systems come with a testing kit, but these are often a separate purchase.

Yes. Each indoor growing system has its own recommendations on how often to clean it, and some systems recommend cleaning as often as once a month. In general, cleaning requires removing all the spent plants and scrubbing or wiping out the unit—especially the water reservoir—before using it again. Apart from that, wipe down the surfaces with a clean, damp rag as necessary to remove dust, plant debris, and grime.

#7697. The Best Lunch Boxes for Construction Workers, Picks from Our Editors

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 11, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Lunch boxes for construction workers need to keep food fresh, but they must also be highly portable and durable to meet the demands of their environments. Fortunately, there are hundreds of models on the market to choose from, whether you’re looking for an insulated option for a cold sandwich and salad or an electric lunch box to keep your food hot.

To help you choose the right construction lunch box from the many options available, we researched the pros and cons of various lunch box materials and designs and reached out to two experts for their opinions. Based on our research and their insights, we chose the Arctic Zone Titan 16 Can Zipperless Hardbody Cooler as our top choice for its tough construction, easy-to-clean interior, and convenient shoulder strap. Below, you’ll find our reviews on the rest of our top picks of the best lunch boxes for construction workers and details on which features matter most when selecting the right one.

Bottom line: Find the perfect lunch box for construction workers with our top picks, balancing durability, portability, and functionality.

The following lunch boxes for work have been assigned different awards to make it easier to focus on specific feature sets. We’ve included everything from heated lunch boxes to those that have a separate compartment or multiple compartments to keep hot meals organized away from water bottles. If you’re looking for gifts for construction workers or a professional lunch box for yourself, our top picks have got you covered.

Choosing the single best lunch box for construction workers was challenging, but the Arctic Zone cooler boasts several user-friendly features, offers good durability, and is also affordable.

At first glance, it looks like a soft-sided cooler, but the exterior fabric contains a solid, leakproof liner that actually makes it a hard-sided model. Its main compartment has a removable SmartShelf you can use to divide the interior space so hard items like water bottles don’t crush soft things like sandwiches The zipper-free lid flips over to provide fast and easy access to the cooler’s contents. There is also an insulated front pocket and a mesh pocket on each end.

The Arctic Zone cooler has a thick base designed to keep ice for up to 2 days. Though the 16-can version has quite a large capacity, it’s actually quite comfortable to carry thanks to its padded, adjustable shoulder strap.

Get the Arctic Zone lunch box for construction workers (various colors and sizes) at Amazon, Target, or Arctic Zone.

Few materials are tougher than steel, and since production costs are relatively low, this Stanley classic lunch box is both rugged and budget-conscious. Though a basic model, it boasts a durable construction and a clip in the lid that can hold Stanley’s classic insulated vacuum bottle or other similar-sized containers. It has two metal latches that provide firm, secure closure and a sturdy handle that makes it easy to carry.

With a 10-quart capacity, there’s ample room for food, but this no-frills hard shell lunch box lacks insulation. So consider this sturdy, well-priced model a solid choice for traditional lunches of sandwiches, subs, and snacks. This model also comes in a few color options to suit individual user preferences.

Get the Stanley Classic lunch box for construction workers (various colors) at Amazon.

Milwaukee is known for its pro-grade jobsite tools, so who better to create a women’s and men’s work lunch box that’s durable enough for heavy-duty conditions? There’s plenty of space inside the high-capacity, soft-sided cooler to hold and food and beverages for a hard day’s work. The dual-layer insulation can keep ice for up to 24 hours, and there are five separate compartments in the lid and sides for dry food and snacks.

The exterior is made of tear-resistant 1680D ballistic material, and this builders’ lunch bag also has a hard, impact-resistant base. All hardware is metal rather than plastic to enable long-term use, and it has a tape measure clip that doubles as a bottle opener as well as a padded shoulder strap.

Get the Milwaukee lunch box for construction workers at Amazon, Ace Hardware, The Home Depot, or Northern Tool + Equipment.

Klein is respected in the construction and contractor trades for producing high-quality hand and power tools, and the brand’s tough Tradesman Pro heavy-duty lunch box maintains that reputation. It features efficient insulation that can keep the contents cool (or warm) for up to 30 hours, and the hard lunch box has a weight rating of up to 300 pounds, which means it can also be used as a seat. Additionally, it has corrosion-proof stainless steel lid hinges that stay open at either 90 or 180 degrees for convenient access as you eat. One side of the lid is recessed to allow 1-liter bottles to stand upright, while the other has a useful compartment for small items like utensils and medications.

There’s a lot we love about the Klein Tools Tradesman Pro cooler, but it does have one design flaw: The strap doubles as the lid closure, but it doesn’t tighten as firmly as it could. While Klein recommends using a padlock to secure the lock hasp, that’s likely unnecessary for most jobsites. However, with its large capacity and long cooling time, this is a great lunch box for guys and gals working long shifts.

Get the Klein Tools lunch box for construction workers at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Northern Tool + Equipment.

Because it’s such an effective thermal box for lunch or even a couple of day’s worth of meals, the appropriately named Igloo takes our award for the best lunch cooler. It is built to withstand the rigors of the construction site and has enough capacity for a whole crew (or your family on the weekend). It has extra-thick, efficient insulation in its body and lid and rubber latches that keep its top tightly closed.

The hard-wearing case features rustproof stainless-steel reinforcements on the handles with rubber grips for comfort. It has a stainless steel kick plate on the front for impact protection as well as oversized skid plates and tie-down points at each corner for secure transportation. Since it does have a 25-quart capacity, however, it may be best used for more than one person or a full day of meals.

Get the Igloo lunch box for construction workers (various colors) at Amazon.

Salads and sandwiches are fine during the summer, but many of us prefer hot meals when the weather starts to get cold. The Travelisimo electric lunch box is the ideal solution for the construction site. It comes with a standard 110V plug suitable for an electrical outlet or a generator. There’s also a 12V/24V vehicle cable that allows users to enjoy a warm meal on the road.

Depending on the power source and the box’s contents, thorough warming takes just 20 to 30 minutes. The outer case prevents you from burning your fingers, and the inner stainless steel container is lightweight and dishwasher safe. This heated lunch box also comes with a carry bag, a fruit box that fits inside, and a stainless steel knife and fork.

Get the Travelisimo lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

When storage space is at a premium—at home, in the vehicle, or on the job—the CleverMade cooler offers an efficient solution. Its 24-can capacity holds a mighty big meal, and the solid base and wire support frame give reasonable structure when in use. It collapses to just 2.75 inches thick, and its patented SnapHinge makes it simple to switch between open and closed.

As a soft-sided cooler, the CleverMade doesn’t have the strength or durability of a hard-sided model, though the lined polyester fabric is lightweight and easy to wipe clean. The lunch box has handles and a strap for convenience, an incorporated bottle opener, and a large mesh pocket. Though the liner is leakproof, the insulated walls of the cooler aren’t super thick, so using blocks of ice might be smart since cubed ice won’t stay frozen long.

Get the CleverMade lunch box for construction workers at Amazon or CleverMade.

Well known for high-quality protective clothing for construction workers, Carhartt has designed its insulated lunch cooler to the same standards. The abrasion-resistant 600 denier polyester is triple stitched and protected by the brand’s Rain Defender water-repellent coating. Its zippers are the same heavyweight YKK versions used on other Carhartt products, including the best construction work pants.

The two main compartments inside this Carhartt deluxe lunch cooler provide versatile food storage and keep contents cool for 8 hours or more. You can access the top section separately from the bottom, and it also has a handy zippered pocket on the front. The bag’s handle and shoulder strap make it easy to carry, though we’re surprised the latter isn’t adjustable. Though obviously not as strong as a hard-sided model, the Carhartt cooler, one of our top lunch coolers for construction workers, is light, surprisingly rugged, and a great value.

Get the Carhartt lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

Those who geek out on refrigerator organization will be happy to know there’s now a jobsite lunch box perfectly adapted to their preferences. The kit comes with six separate food containers (two 1.5-cup and four 2.5-cup containers), a 23-ounce shaker cup with a whisk, screw-on storage pots for supplements or protein powders, and a 7-day pill dispenser. The bag itself has a mesh pocket inside the front flap, a pocket outside, and an end pocket for the shaker cup as well as a top handle and an adjustable shoulder strap for convenient carrying. Two cooling blocks complete the comprehensive package.

Getting everything inside is a tight squeeze, and we are a little concerned about the long-term durability of the bag in tough environments. But if you like to keep all your items separate and organized and don’t mind that some of the containers are on the small side, the ThinkFit meal prep lunch bag set will be hard to beat.

Get the ThinkFit lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

Good lunch boxes for construction workers come in all shapes and sizes, and the Tourit soft backpack cooler is a larger option that’s easy to strap to your back so your hands are free for other tools and supplies. It’s made from durable, vented waterproof fabric and has a padded back as well as padded shoulder straps. The interior features an insulated high-density foam paired with a leak-resistant liner.

Pack hot or cold food inside, and the insulation will hold the food’s temperature for up to 16 hours. Rather than using cubed ice, however, the manufacturer recommends using reusable ice packs to ensure liquids don’t leak from the zipper. In addition to its 30-can main compartment, this backpack cooler has multiple top, front, and side pockets to store not only food and drink but necessary items like your phone, keys, and wallet.

Get the Tourit lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

To choose the right lineup of lunch boxes for the varying needs of construction workers, we considered the amount of food and drink each option could carry as well as the holding temperatures they could maintain to keep consumable items safe and fresh. Durability and portability were also top priorities, as these lunch bags and boxes must be convenient to carry yet strong enough to hold up to rugged jobsites. Though we were also careful about selecting options to fit a range of budgets, we ruled out cheaply made, low-quality lunch boxes in favor of products that offer lasting value for long-term use.

Shawna Guevara, managing director at Landmark Structural Builders, confirms much of our own thinking. “A proper lunch box for construction workers should prioritize functionality and durability,” she says. “Workers don’t need zippers that break easily, lunch boxes that retain food odors, or ones that are difficult to clean.”

As you decide which lunch box is right for you, consider these expert insights from contractor Jay Sanders of remodeling specialists Maryland Contractors regarding which features to look for when shopping for women’s and men’s lunch boxes for work. For Jay, “a tight-fitting lid that keeps food at the desired temperature for hours” and “chemical-free lunch boxes for meals that don’t harm your health” are the most important considerations.

Since lunch boxes designed for the office or coolers for the beach may not stand up to the rigors of the jobsite, evaluating construction worker lunch boxes based on the following key elements will ensure you get the right product for your needs.

Lunch boxes aren’t always treated with the greatest care. Those that have a tough outer shell will be more resistant to damage from the knocks and bumps that are part of life on a busy construction site. Hard-sided lunch boxes can help prevent food from getting smashed, and some are even strong enough to sit on while you eat. Though they are more durable, their construction can make them a bit heavier, bulkier, and less portable.

On the other hand, soft-sided and collapsible coolers are quite portable. They’re almost always lighter than hard models, are a snap to store, and are frequently less expensive. Though soft-sided coolers don’t provide as much protection for their contents as hard options, a soft lunch box can be a perfectly viable option if your lunch will wait in a vehicle rather than be toted directly to the site.

Capacity requirements largely depend on how big a meal you typically pack. A larger capacity may be more versatile—it can be used for a family weekend outing, for example. Conversely, the best small coolers will be sized just right for single-meal use as well as more portable and easier to store.

Capacity descriptions vary. Often, they are given as a number of standard beverage cans, making capacity fairly easy to visualize. Quart capacity is another common measurement. Those given in inches can make it difficult to picture the true size, so it may be smart to fold some cardboard into roughly the measurements given to avoid ordering a lunch box that’s too small or large.

Multiple compartments (as often found in bento boxes) are convenient for those who take various items for lunch and wish to keep them separated. One of our top picks even includes a pill organizer.

A well-insulated construction lunch box can keep food cool or warm for some time. However, while some manufacturers indicate how long they expect the contents to maintain temperature, their estimates may be optimistic, and there isn’t any recognized standard for the amount of insulation a lunch box or cooler provides. Shoppers should use their best judgment: Look at the thickness of the insulation, how rugged the fabric and seams are, and how well the insulated area closes.

How a construction worker lunch box is carried and how easily it opens and closes is also worth considering, so examine the soundness of handles and clasps. Those likely to pack ice in the lunch box should also check how leakproof it is, particularly with soft cool boxes.

All aspects of jobsite safety are important—even regarding your lunch box. Certain products previously used to produce plastics are now deemed unsafe for use with food. The organic compound bisphenol A (known as BPA) is one of the main culprits, though PVC and phthalates (which make plastics more flexible) should also be avoided. Many manufacturers will state whether their plastic containers are free of these materials. Since food hygiene is a crucial part of food safety, remember also to consider how easy it will be to thoroughly wash all areas of the container.

The guide above contains useful information and vetted products to help you choose the best lunch box for construction workers. Anyone with additional questions about how to choose and use a rugged, reliable lunch box will find more information below.

As with the best coolers, keeping lunch cold in a lunch box is best accomplished by using an insulated ice bag or box with ice blocks or bags of ice inside.

Hot soups and stews will maintain the desired temperature inside an insulated container or vacuum bottle. Plug-in warmers like the Travelisimo Electric Heated Lunch Box can also heat meals so long as a wall outlet or DC port is available.

The body can absorb aluminum through contact with food. However, many sources say it passes through naturally and does not present health problems. Some aluminum lunch boxes are specifically marked as food safe.

The best way to clean most lunch boxes is with a sponge and warm, soapy water, though the manufacturer may have its own suggestions, and these should take priority.

Health experts often suggest you replace your lunch box every year since even the best options can accumulate small amounts of mold and bacteria in hard-to-clean crevices. If damaged, a lunch box should be replaced immediately to prevent any risk of contamination.

Generally speaking, no, lunch boxes are not microwavable. If you need a microwavable container, consider packing something like these PrepNaturals glass meal-prep containers inside your lunch box.

Stainless steel lunch boxes aren’t necessarily better than plastic ones. However, they are a lightweight and durable option, especially for construction workers. This Stanley Classic 10-Quart Lunch Box is one of our absolute favorite steel lunch boxes.

Whether you’re shopping for a new homeowner or a serious hobbyist, we’ve got a gift idea for you.
